why: A rigorous Stein–Chen bound in a probabilistic model over random p (averaged) is achievable and gives the correct 'zero probability' heuristic with error terms.
first_step: Define the model with p uniform in a residue class mod large M; compute Stein–Chen dependency neighbourhoods and TV bound.

title: Second moment method over primes in short intervals: positive proportion with R(p) ≥ 1 in every interval
connection: Paley–Zygmund on R over primes in [X, X+H] ↔ ES almost-all in short intervals.
why: Repo has interval results; second moment at H = (log X)^A would be a new 'every short interval contains many ES primes' result (weak but new form).
first_step: Check repo's (D)30 interval result range of H; compute what second moment would need for H = (log X)^A.

title: Dynamics on the space of lattices: ES certificates as cusp excursions of a p-indexed orbit
connection: Orbits of diagonal flows on SL₃(ℝ)/SL₃(ℤ) visiting the cusp correspond to small vectors ↔ ES certificates are small vectors in p-dependent lattices.
why: Cusp excursions are governed by Diophantine properties; Littlewood-type pointwise statements are hard but some (Einsiedler–Katok–Lindenstrauss) give measure results.
first_step: Write a 3D lattice Λ_p such that a vector in a specified small cone ⟹ certificate; examine whether the a-orbit of Λ_p is known to enter the cusp region.

title: Littlewood conjecture analogy: inf n‖nα‖‖nβ‖ = 0 vs ES certificates as simultaneous small values
connection: Both ask for simultaneous small values of products of distances ↔ ES Type II p ≡ −(u+B) mod 4uB is a multiplicative Diophantine approximation condition.
why: Littlewood is open too, with measure-zero exceptional set (EKL) — a parallel of 'almost all' ES results; methods might transfer in either direction.
first_step: Write ES Type II as a product-of-distances condition and compare its structure with Littlewood's.

title: Bohr sets / Bohr neighbourhoods of p: certificates as elements of a Bohr set
connection: Bohr set B(Γ,ε) = {x : ‖γx‖ < ε} ↔ ES certificates require p/m near −u/m exactly (ε = 0).
why: Additive-combinatorics machinery on Bohr sets gives structure for 'approximate' ES; exact would need ε < 1/m.
first_step: Compute, per p, the approximate certificate count with tolerance ε = k/m for k ≤ K and check if exact count ≈ approximate/(2K+1).

title: Self-organised criticality: hardest primes as avalanche precursors in the sieve
connection: SOC/avalanche models ↔ the number of residue-filter stages needed per prime (heavy-tailed?).
why: If the stage-count distribution is power-law, extrapolation to large p is different from exponential; matters for P(ES false) estimates.
first_step: Record, for verification filters, the number of filter stages before a prime is resolved; plot tail distribution.

title: Annealed vs quenched averages for certificate counts
connection: Disordered systems: quenched average E[log Z] vs annealed log E[Z] ↔ log R(p) average vs log of average.
why: A large gap indicates rare-event dominance (some p with huge counts, e.g. via Linnik), which affects lower-tail heuristics.
first_step: Compute E[log(1+R(p))] vs log E[R(p)] over primes in dyadic ranges up to 10⁸.

title: Replica trick / cavity method for counting solutions of a sparse arithmetic CSP
connection: Belief propagation counts solutions of sparse CSPs (k-SAT) accurately ↔ ES as a CSP in digits of (u,B,C).
why: BP on a digit-level CSP gives an independent estimate of R(p) that might capture correlations missing from the naive model.
first_step: Encode 4uBC − u − B = p in binary with carries; run BP solution-count estimate (e.g. via a #SAT approx counter) for p ~ 10⁶ and compare with exact R(p).

title: Zeta-function regularisation of Σ_{u,C} 1/(4uC−1) as continuum main term
connection: Main term M₀ ~ (3/(2π²)) log² p from Σ 1/φ(4uB) ↔ Epstein-type zeta functions; regularised values give constant terms.
why: Exact secondary terms (log p and constant) sharpen the empirical comparison and the zero-probability model.
first_step: Derive the full asymptotic M₀(p) = a log²p + b log p + c + o(1) via Mellin transform; check against computed values.

title: Chaotic dynamics: the 'Egyptian map' T(a/b) = a/b − 1/⌈b/a⌉ and its periodic structure mod p
connection: Iterating the greedy step on all a/p, a ∈ (ℤ/p)^× defines a map on residues ↔ ES asks about orbits of length ≤ 3 from a = 4 through rescaled fractions.
why: Graph structure of this map on F_p (functional graph) could have computable statistics (tree sizes) related to ES.
first_step: Build the functional graph of the greedy-remainder map on fractions with denominator dividing p·k for small k; compute statistics.

title: Hydrodynamic limit of certificate count as p → ∞ along residue classes
connection: Limit shape of the set of successful (log u/log p, log C/log p) ↔ the main-term density.
why: A limit shape theorem (empirical measure of certificates converges) for almost all p is plausibly provable and would describe where certificates live.
first_step: Plot the empirical measure of (log u, log C)/log p for successful pairs over many p; compare with 1/(uC) density prediction.

title: Benjamini–Schramm / local limit of the 'divisor graph' around p
connection: Local weak limits of graphs ↔ the neighbourhood structure of p in the ES certificate graph.
why: Too abstract unless a concrete graph emerges; keep as curiosity.
first_step: Define graph: vertices = primes ≤ X, edge p~q if they share a certificate modulus; compute degree distribution.

title: Quantum algorithm: Grover search for certificates and complexity of certification
connection: Grover gives √ speedup for unstructured search ↔ ES certificate search space ~ p log p trials, polylog winners.
why: Not a proof route; clarifies computational complexity of finding a certificate (classical best ~ ?).
first_step: Determine the best classical algorithm complexity for finding one ES solution for a given p (repo/verification code) and record whether it's polylog-time heuristically.

title: Shor-type period finding: ES certificate as a hidden-subgroup instance?
connection: HSP over (ℤ/N)^× ↔ ES gate: subgroup generated by divisor classes containing −1.
why: Curiosity mapping; might reveal that certificate-finding reduces to factoring 4Cp+1 (which it does) — so ES search ∈ BQP-easy given factoring.
first_step: Write explicit reduction: ES(p) certificate search ≤ factoring of numbers 4Cp+1 for C ≤ polylog — then note quantum polynomial time.

title: Coppersmith small-root method for the bilinear certificate equation
connection: p = 4uCk − u − k (for fixed u, unknowns C,k) ↔ Coppersmith/Howgrave-Graham find small roots of bivariate polynomials modulo unknown divisors.
why: Coppersmith gives pointwise existence/finding of small roots when a size condition holds; if the size condition covers the ES certificate size range, the lattice gives a constructive certificate finder with provable bounds (likely the condition fails; quantify by how much).
first_step: Set up f(C,k) = 4uCk − u − k − p and compute the Coppersmith bound X·Y ≤ p^δ for which small roots are guaranteed to be found; compare with expected certificate sizes (C,k ≤ ?).

title: Factoring with hints: ES as 'find a factor of 4Cp+1 in a residue class' (Coppersmith known-MSB/LSB attacks)
connection: Coppersmith factors N given half the bits of a factor; ES wants a factor of N_C = 4Cp+1 ≡ −1 mod 4C — i.e. the low bits (mod 4C) of the factor are known.
why: Known-LSB factoring (factors in a prescribed class mod M with M ≥ N^{1/4}) is polynomial time via lattices; ES's modulus 4C is tiny relative to N^{1/4}, but summing over C gives many tries.
first_step: Quantify: for which C is 4C ≥ (4Cp+1)^{1/4}? (C ≥ p^{1/3}) — then Coppersmith decides existence of a factor ≡ −1 mod 4C exactly; check whether the large-C range alone has certificates often (data).

title: Lenstra's 'divisors in residue classes' theorem: at most a bounded number of divisors ≡ r mod s when s > N^{1/3}
connection: Lenstra (1984): if s > N^{1/3}, N has ≤ 11 divisors ≡ r mod s, computable in poly time ↔ ES divisor form d | 4Cp+1, d ≡ −1 mod 4C; Coppersmith–Howgrave-Graham–Nagaraj extended to s > N^{1/4}.
why: Repo has s3_lll_lenstra (prior art). Upper bounds, not existence; but the algorithmic side lets us decide each large-C slice exactly — useful for adversarial verification at astronomical p.
first_step: Check repo's s3_lll_lenstra memo; implement the CHN algorithm for slices with C ≥ p^{1/3} and measure hit rates for p ~ 10^30.

title: SAT encoding of 'no certificate up to size B' for a symbolic p (bit-blasted) to search for counterexample shapes
connection: Encode: p prime-ish (or just p ≡ 1 mod 840) and ∀ small certificates fail, as a SAT/SMT instance over bits of p ↔ counterexample search.
why: SAT solvers find structured satisfying assignments quickly; UNSAT for bounded p-size would be a verification certificate; SAT gives adversarial p for testing.
first_step: Encode in Z3/bitwuzla: p 64-bit, p ≡ 1 mod 840, and for all (u,C) ≤ 20, (4uC−1) ∤ p+u; ask for a model; then check those p for full ES.

title: CRT-construction of adversarial p evading all small certificates (Chinese remainder adversary)
connection: Choose p mod Π(4uC−1) avoiding −u for all small (u,C) ↔ B1 barrier; the smallest such p as function of the menu bound.
why: Gives the 'cost' of evading menu of size B; growth rate of the minimal evader vs actual certificate sizes calibrates how big the menu must be at p.
first_step: Compute minimal prime p ≡ 1 mod 840 avoiding all (u,C) with 4uC−1 ≤ B for B = 10..200 via CRT + sieve; plot log p vs B.

title: Proof complexity: does ES for p ≤ N have short resolution/cutting-plane certificates?
connection: Each ES(p) has a polynomial-size certificate (x,y,z) ↔ 'ES for all p ≤ N' has a certificate of size N·polylog; the question is whether a uniform short proof exists — Π₁ statements and bounded arithmetic.
why: Bounded arithmetic (S¹₂, IΔ₀) characterisations: if ES were provable in IΔ₀+Ω₁, there would be polynomial-time witnessing — certificate finding in poly(log p) time. This turns a proof-theoretic question into an algorithmic one.
first_step: Read Buss witnessing theorem; formulate 'ES provable in S¹₂ ⟹ poly(log p)-time certificate algorithm'. Test: is there a heuristic poly(log p) algorithm for certificates (yes, try small C)? Is it provably correct?

title: Witnessing theorem contrapositive: if certificate-finding is hard (e.g. needs factoring), ES is not provable in weak arithmetic
connection: Divisor-form certificates need factoring 4Cp+1 ↔ if every certificate search needs factoring, ES ∉ provable in S¹₂ (under crypto assumptions).
why: Gives a meta-theorem: proofs must use non-constructive or strong tools; clarifies why elementary attempts fail.
first_step: Check whether ES certificates can be found without factoring (e.g. via the Type I trial form, which needs only divisibility tests, poly-time per trial). If yes, the obstruction vanishes.

title: Average-case complexity: certificate search as a TFNP problem
connection: If ES is true, 'given p, find (x,y,z)' is a total search problem ↔ TFNP classes (PPA, PPAD, PPP, PLS).
why: Membership in PPA/PPP etc. corresponds to the existence proof style (parity, pigeonhole). Classifying ES-search would point to the proof principle needed (cf. Fermat two squares ∈ PPA? and Zagier involution ⇒ PPA-like).
first_step: Read 'TFNP and number theory' (Papadimitriou; Ban et al. on PPA and factoring; Sotiraki–Zampetakis–Zirdelis PPP) and try to place ES-search: is there a parity argument (PPA) or pigeonhole (PPP)?

title: Two-squares in PPA (Zagier windmill) ↔ ES in PPA? A search-problem formulation of windmills
connection: Finding x²+y² = p is in PPA via the Zagier involution (and is known poly-time via Cornacchia) ↔ ES windmill involutions would put ES-search in PPA.
why: If ES-search were PPA-hard or PPA-complete under a natural encoding, that would mean ES's proof must be a parity argument — direct guidance.
first_step: Check the literature on 'Fermat two squares' complexity class membership (e.g. Goldberg–?); attempt to write an ES windmill as a PPA instance (a graph of degree ≤ 2 with p-dependent vertices).

title: Pigeonhole (PPP) certificate: injectively map a set of size > N into a set of size N
connection: PPP problems: pigeonhole collisions ↔ ES certificates from a collision in a map from (thick set) to (smaller set) where collisions are certificates.
why: Thue's lemma is a PPP-style argument; ES via a collision would be a G1 'collision' column cell.
first_step: Look for a map from a set of size ≍ p (e.g. residues a mod p) to a set of size < p whose collisions yield (u,B,C) — test candidates on small p.

title: Program synthesis: search for a short program f(p) → (x,y,z) correct for all p ≤ 10⁸
connection: Program synthesis (e.g. enumerative, stochastic superoptimisation, LLM-guided) ↔ a uniform algorithm with provable termination would be ES.
why: Any synthesised program with a bounded loop is a finite menu (B1, must fail i.o. under Dickson); but unbounded-loop programs with simple invariants could suggest a proof structure.
first_step: Run a DSL search (loops over small parameter, modular tests) for programs certifying all primes ≤ 10⁶ with minimal description length; inspect top programs for invariants.

title: Termination analysis tools (ranking functions) applied to an ES search loop
connection: Software verification proves loop termination via ranking functions ↔ ES ⟺ 'for c := 1,2,… test certificate(p,c)' terminates for all p.
why: Automated termination provers (AProVE, Ultimate) fail on number theory, but the framing exposes what invariant is needed: a ranking function = a quantity decreasing until success.
first_step: Write the search loop in C and run a termination analyser to see what it asks for (expect failure; record the missing invariant).

title: Automata: is the set of p (in base b) with a certificate of size ≤ B a regular language? (Büchi/Cobham)
connection: Sets defined by finitely many congruence conditions are b-automatic ↔ finite menus give automatic sets; ES (all primes) is not automatic but the complement of a finite menu is.
why: Cobham's theorem: automatic in two multiplicatively independent bases ⟹ ultimately periodic. Menus are periodic; any 'digital' certificate rule (digit-carry algorithms, B1 hatch) gives automatic sets in one base only — a way to classify digit-based ideas.
first_step: Take a digit-carry ES rule (repo E2 hatch) and compute its automaton; check whether its success set is periodic (then B1) or genuinely base-dependent.

title: Walnut theorem prover for automatic-sequence statements about ES menus
connection: Walnut (Shallit) decides first-order statements about automatic sequences ↔ menu-coverage statements are automatic.
why: Fast way to prove/disprove finite-menu coverings rigorously (although B1 says they fail on primes, Walnut can check for structured n like 4^s + k families).
first_step: Encode the repo's 4^s + k family proofs in Walnut (base 4 automatic) as a test, then try open 4^s + 297 or 15·2^s + 1 families.

title: Lattice attacks on 'hidden number problem' as a model for finding u with p ≡ −u mod (4uC−1)
connection: HNP: recover hidden α from approximations of α·t mod q ↔ ES conditions as simultaneous approximations.
why: Cryptanalysis has fine-tuned lattice dimensions/bounds for such problems; reuse could design efficient certificate finders for huge p.
first_step: Write ES Type II as approximations of p/(4uC−1) to integers; try a BKZ-based search for certificates at p ~ 10^40 and compare yield with brute force.

title: ECM-style randomised factoring of 4Cp+1 tuned to divisors ≡ −1 mod 4C
connection: ECM finds small factors; ES only needs some divisor in a class ↔ certificate search at astronomical p.
why: Engineering: lets adversarial searches reach p ~ 10^100 cheaply (only smooth parts needed).
first_step: Implement: for C ≤ 10⁴, pull small factors of 4Cp+1 by trial division/ECM and test subproducts for class −1 mod 4C; measure success rate at p ~ 10^100.

title: Index calculus analogy: smooth relations and linear algebra over (ℤ/4C)^×
connection: Index calculus finds discrete logs by collecting smooth relations ↔ ES gate: express −1 as a product of factor-base primes' classes, with the factor base = small primes dividing p-tied integers.
why: Linear algebra over exponent vectors mod the group exponent makes 'is −1 in the generated subgroup' decidable; collecting relations across many C might show the subgroup is always everything.
first_step: For hard p, collect smooth parts of 4Cp+1 for C ≤ 10³; for each C compute the subgroup generated mod 4C; record when it's proper.

title: Lattice of exponent vectors: ES certificate as short vector in a relation lattice
connection: Repo gon_lll_relation_lattice ↔ relation lattices among divisor classes.
why: Already explored in repo; listing for coverage. New angle: use LLL to find a subproduct with prescribed class AND size constraint simultaneously.
first_step: Read BRAINSTORM/gon_lll_relation_lattice.md; check whether the size constraint (d < √N) was included in the lattice.

title: Model checking / BDDs for residue-class coverage up to large modulus
connection: Binary decision diagrams represent huge residue-class sets compactly ↔ the uncovered set after modular filters.
why: Exact representation of the uncovered set mod M (M huge) enables precise density of residual primes and structure detection.
first_step: Represent uncovered residues mod 840·Π small primes as a BDD over CRT digits; measure size growth.

title: ILP / MIP solvers on the ES Diophantine equation with bounds
connection: Integer programming with nonlinear constraints ↔ certificate search; branch-and-bound gives infeasibility certificates for bounded boxes.
why: Infeasibility certificates (dual bounds) for 'no certificate in box' are mechanical proofs of local non-existence; could expose structure in hard primes.
first_step: Formulate 4xyz = p(xy+yz+zx) with x ≤ y ≤ z bounds in a MINLP solver (SCIP) for p=409 restricted to Type II (★) and inspect the infeasibility proof.

title: Cryptographic hardness assumption: 'ES-certificate search is hard' as a one-way function candidate
connection: If certificates were hard to find but easy to verify, p ↦ certificate is a NP-search; crypto reductions require average-case hardness ↔ ES almost-all results suggest easy on average.
why: Fun meta: certificate search is easy heuristically (small C works), so ES gives no OWF; that easiness itself is evidence of a uniform algorithm.
first_step: Quantify: over primes ≤ 10⁹, distribution of the work (number of trials) to find the first certificate; if max work is polylog, conjecture a 'polylog search time' strengthening.

title: Strengthened conjecture: first certificate found within O(log² p) trials in a canonical order
connection: Stronger statement 'ES with an explicit search bound' ↔ like Linnik's constant or least-prime-in-AP bounds.
why: Stronger, more rigid conjectures are sometimes easier to attack (induction/structure) or to refute (giving insight). Also gives a cheap computational target.
first_step: Fix canonical order on (u,C) by 4uC−1; compute max over p ≤ 10⁹ of the index of first success / log² p.

title: Least-quadratic-non-residue analogue: 'least certificate' function and its Burgess-type bound
connection: n₂(p) ≪ p^{1/(4√e)+ε} (Burgess–Vinogradov) ↔ least certificate size ℓ(p); repo connects F_q forcing lines to n₂(p).
why: A Burgess-type 'least certificate ≤ p^θ' bound would be a theorem implying ES! (any finite bound). The analogy shows which tool (character sums over short intervals) would apply if the certificate condition were character-like.
first_step: Write the certificate indicator as a combination of characters mod moduli of size ≤ p^θ and check whether short character sum bounds could give existence for θ < 1 (probably fails due to tied moduli — record precisely where).

title: Miller–Rabin witness analogy: deterministic witness sets under GRH (Bach) vs ES certificates
connection: Under GRH the least Miller–Rabin witness is ≤ 2 log² n (Bach) ↔ ES: under GRH, is the least certificate ≤ polylog?
why: Bach's bound comes from GRH ⟹ characters can't all be trivial on [1, 2log²n]; ES's analogue would need certificates to be detected by characters with non-tied moduli.
first_step: Formulate a GRH-conditional statement of the form 'some character condition on primes ≤ log² p ⟹ certificate' and test on data (e.g. (ℓ/p) = −1 for ℓ in a fixed set).

title: Learning-with-errors / lattice duality analogy: no
connection: LWE hardness vs ES certificate search ↔ superficial: both involve modular linear relations.
why: Probably vacuous; kept low confidence as a pointer that lattice duality (transference) could convert 'no certificate' into 'short dual vector' — a dual certificate of failure.
first_step: Formulate: if no certificate in lattice coset, transference gives a short dual vector; compute dual vectors for (★)-failing p = 409 and see if they look structured.

title: Dual certificates of failure: what does a 'proof of no Type II (★) solution' look like for p = 409?
connection: Each (★)-failing prime has a finite proof of failure (exhaustion) ↔ shortest such proof structure (via sieving modulo few primes?) reveals what a counterexample to ES would require.
why: If (★)-failures always have short structured proofs (e.g. via a few congruences), then ES-failure needs a similar compact obstruction pattern, which might be ruled out.
first_step: For the 14 (★)-failing primes, compute the minimal set of residue checks proving failure (it's a covering of the trial set); look for common shape.

title: Interactive proofs: verifier checks ES for random p quickly — PCP-style 'ES holds on a dense set' certificates
connection: Probabilistically checkable statements ↔ almost-all ES; verifying 'ES for all p ≤ N' needs a list; can one compress the list into a short certificate (e.g. a few polynomial identities + exceptions)?
why: Compression of the verification certificate is equivalent to finding uniform structure; measuring compressibility (MDL) of the verification list is an experimental structure probe.
first_step: Take the list of minimal certificates for p ≤ 10⁷ and compute how many 'polynomial-family rules' are needed to cover 99%, 99.9%, … (greedy set cover).

title: Greedy set cover of primes by polynomial certificate families (Mordell-style) — coverage decay curve
connection: Families (identities valid on residue classes) cover primes; set-cover curve shows diminishing returns ↔ B1 says never 100%.
why: The decay exponent of the uncovered fraction vs number of families is a quantitative fingerprint; compare with sieve dimension predictions.
first_step: Generate the identity families from ET parametrisations with small parameters; run greedy cover over primes ≤ 10⁸; fit uncovered fraction vs #families.

title: Distributed computing / BOINC-style verification to 10^19 or 10^20
connection: Verification frontier 10^18 ↔ volunteer computing (like PrimeGrid) could extend it; also gives data on hardest primes.
why: Not proof progress, but extends EVIDENCE and adversarial data; community engagement.
first_step: Estimate cost: Mihnea–Dumitru's runtime per 10^18 and the extension cost; check PrimeGrid/yoyo@home interest in number-theory side projects.

title: GPU kernel for (★)/I3 census to 10^12
connection: Repo census to 10^10 single engine ↔ GPU acceleration for residue-filter checks.
why: Extends CERTIFIED data for I3_𝒞 and (★) failures; tests growth of least u.
first_step: Port scripts/z52_bank_i3c.c inner loop to CUDA; benchmark on 10^10..10^10+10^8.

title: Formal verification: Lean proof of Mordell's mod-840 reduction and of 'ES for n ≤ 10^4' by decide
connection: Lean/mathlib formalisation ↔ repo results; erdosproblems/formal-conjectures repo has an ES statement?
why: Formal statements and reductions lower the cost for AI provers and guard against errors; cheap community contribution.
first_step: Check google-deepmind/formal-conjectures for Erdős–Straus statement; contribute Lean proof of the 4/n reduction to primes ≡ 1 mod 4 if missing.

title: Lean formalisation of the T1 odd-square obstruction (Type I/II empty at odd squares)
connection: T1 is a clean reciprocity statement ↔ a formal proof makes it a reusable test in automated pipelines.
why: Formal T1 lets AI provers automatically reject approaches that would prove T1-false statements.
first_step: Write Lean statement: ∀ m odd, ¬∃ (Type II coprime solution) for 4/m²; prove via Jacobi symbol reciprocity in mathlib.

title: Automated conjecture generation (Graffiti / TxGraffiti / Ramanujan Machine) on ES statistics
connection: Ramanujan Machine-style search for formulas ↔ conjecture identities for M(p), R(p) moments, minimal certificates.
why: Automated conjecturing may find unexpected exact relations (e.g. between R(p) and class numbers).
first_step: Feed (p, R(p), h(−4p), h(4p), ε_p, n₂(p), Ω(p±1), …) for p ≤ 10⁶ into a Graffiti-like inequality-conjecturer; inspect outputs.

title: Symbolic regression (PySR) on the minimal-certificate size function
connection: Fit min-certificate size ℓ(p) or R(p) as symbolic expression in features of p ↔ discovering hidden dependencies.
why: Cheap; negative result also informative (ℓ(p) is 'random').
first_step: Run PySR with features (log p, p mod small m, Ω(p+k), Legendre symbols) on 10⁵ primes; report best formulas and residual variance.

title: Gradient-boosted classifier predicting (★)-line failure from residues: feature importance
connection: ML classifier on p's residues mod m ≤ M predicting low R(p) ↔ which local data matter.
why: Feature importance reveals unexpected moduli or quadratic characters that drive difficulty, possibly a new invariant.
first_step: Train XGBoost on primes ≤ 10⁸ with target log R(p)/log²p, features = p mod m for m ≤ 200 and (q/p) for q ≤ 100; list top features.

title: Neural network certificate generator (learned guessing of (u,C))
connection: Train a model to propose (u,C) for given p, verify exactly ↔ learned certificates.
why: If a small model achieves near-100% top-k accuracy, its learned function may be interpretable (e.g. a rule based on p mod something + a search) — mechanistic interpretability as hypothesis generation.
first_step: Train a transformer on (digits of p) → (u,C) of the smallest certificate for 10⁷ primes; measure top-10 hit rate; probe what it uses.

title: Mechanistic interpretability of a model that 'solves' ES on all tested p
connection: If a network generalises perfectly on out-of-range p, its circuit is an algorithm ↔ a candidate uniform proof idea.
why: Grokking literature shows networks learn modular arithmetic via Fourier features; an ES-solving network would reveal which characters/moduli matter.
first_step: After training (previous item), apply Fourier analysis to embeddings (as in Nanda et al. grokking) to find dominant frequencies.

title: FunSearch-style evolutionary program search for ES certificate heuristics
connection: DeepMind FunSearch used LLM-evolved programs to find cap set constructions ↔ evolve a program mapping p → certificate minimising failures/cost.
why: Evolved programs can reveal compact heuristics; any program with unbounded but structured search may suggest invariants.
first_step: Set up an evolutionary loop (LLM proposes Python functions) scoring by #primes ≤ 10⁶ solved in ≤ k trials; inspect the best programs.

title: AlphaProof/LLM-prover attempts on ES sub-lemmas (e.g. I3 for structured p families)
connection: AI provers now solve Erdős problems of 'abundance' shape ↔ ES sub-lemmas with explicit families (15·2^s+1, 4^s+297).
why: Open thin families are concrete, bounded-difficulty targets suitable for AI+Lean pipelines.
first_step: Formulate 'ES holds for all 15·2^s + 1' as a Lean statement and give it to an AI prover with repo's window technique as hints.

title: Satisfiability modulo theories with nonlinear integer arithmetic: prove 'ES for n ≡ r mod M' identities automatically
connection: SMT (Z3 NIA) can verify polynomial identities with divisibility ↔ automatic discovery of Mordell-type identities for new classes (non-square).
why: Automated rediscovery of all identity classes mod larger moduli maps exactly which classes have identities (Mordell–Schinzel says square classes never do).
first_step: Use a template x = (a n + b)/c etc. and let a solver search coefficients making 4/n = … an identity on a residue class mod 4·k; enumerate classes covered mod 9240.

title: Gröbner bases for parametrised families of ES solutions
connection: Polynomial parametrisations x(t), y(t), z(t) with 4/n(t) identity ↔ Gröbner elimination finds all low-degree families.
why: Systematic enumeration of degree-≤d rational curve families on the generic fibre; complements Mordell–Schinzel.
first_step: Set up unknown-coefficient degree-2 polynomials x(t),y(t),z(t),n(t) and solve the identity via Gröbner; list families and their n-images.

title: Constraint propagation à la Sudoku: residue constraints that a counterexample must satisfy, propagated mod many primes
connection: A counterexample p must avoid all certificate classes; propagating mod q for each q gives allowed residues ↔ CSP over CRT.
why: The density of allowed residues after propagation across q ≤ Q estimates how 'thin' the counterexample class is; if it decays faster than 1/log, the density heuristic sharpens.
first_step: Compute, for each q ≤ 200, the allowed residues of p mod q given all certificates with modulus q; multiply densities.

title: Hash-based birthday search for collisions between Type I and Type II slices
connection: Birthday paradox: two large lists collide ↔ ES via matching a Type I partial with a Type II partial (meet-in-the-middle).
why: Meet-in-the-middle reformulations sometimes convert existence into collision guarantees (G1 collision column).
first_step: Find a decomposition ES(p) ⟺ L1(p) ∩ L2(p) ≠ ∅ with |L1|,|L2| ≍ √p range; test sizes and collision counts.

title: Cellular automaton encoding of the sieve of certificate classes
connection: 1D cellular automaton marking residues ↔ pictures of the uncovered set.
why: Visual exploration; unlikely to yield theorems but cheap pattern-finding.
first_step: Render a 2D image: row = modulus m = 4uC−1, column = p mod m, highlight −u; overlay hard primes.

title: Kolmogorov–Arnold / sparse regression on Fourier coefficients of 1[R(p) small]
connection: Fourier analysis over (ℤ/M)^× of the indicator of hard primes ↔ which characters correlate with difficulty.
why: Large Fourier coefficients identify characters (e.g. quartic residue symbols) beyond quadratic ones that influence R(p).
first_step: Compute Σ_{p hard} χ(p) for all characters χ mod M ≤ 10⁴ (normalised) and list outliers.

title: Quartic and higher residue symbols as hidden invariants of hard primes
connection: Hard primes are ≡ 1 mod 840 (splitting completely in ℚ(ζ_840)); next-order invariants could be quartic/octic residue symbols ↔ e.g. (2/p)_4, (3/p)_4.
why: If (★)-failures cluster on a quartic-symbol class, it's a new structural fact (like F_q forcing lines but higher order).
first_step: For the 14 (★)-failing primes and hardest ES primes, compute (2/p)_4, (3/p)_4, (5/p)_4, (7/p)_4 and compare with random p ≡ 1 mod 840.

title: Hooley's Δ-function: concentration of divisors of 4Cp+1 in short multiplicative intervals
connection: Hooley Δ(N) = max_t #{d | N : t < d ≤ et} ↔ ES wants a divisor in a residue class, not an interval; but divisors-in-classes and divisors-in-intervals are dual via characters.
why: Results like 'Δ(N) is large for most N' (Tenenbaum, Maier–Tenenbaum, Ford–Green–Koukoulopoulos) concern single integers' divisor distributions — closer in spirit to ES's single-integer problem than averaged results.
first_step: Read Ford–Green–Koukoulopoulos 'Equal sums in random sets and the concentration of divisors' (arXiv) and ask for the analogue 'divisors of N in a given class mod q'.

title: Erdős–Hall: divisors of N equidistributed mod q for almost all N
connection: Distribution of divisors of N in residue classes mod q (Erdős–Hall, Hall's book 'Divisors') ↔ ES needs class −1 mod 4C among divisors of 4Cp+1.
why: Results proving 'for almost all N, divisors hit every class mod q when τ(N) ≫ q^{1+ε}' give: ES(p) holds whenever some 4Cp+1 has many divisors relative to C — a structural sufficient condition.
first_step: Find a theorem of the form: if τ(N) ≥ q^A and N has no small prime-power obstruction, then divisors of N cover (ℤ/q)^×; check its proof's dependence (it's essentially Davenport-constant).

title: ES(p) from a single highly composite p-tied integer: smooth 4Cp+1
connection: If 4Cp+1 is very smooth (many small prime factors), its divisors cover (ℤ/4C)^× by zero-sum theory ↔ existence of C ≤ polylog with 4Cp+1 smooth is a smooth-numbers-in-AP question.
why: Smooth values of linear polynomials 4Cp+1 for C in a range: Ψ-in-AP results (Granville, Harper) give existence for C up to p^ε-ish but not polylog; quantify the gap.
first_step: Compute, for hard primes, min over C ≤ 10⁴ of the largest prime factor of 4Cp+1 relative to the requirement Ω ≥ D((ℤ/4C)^×) ; record gap.

title: Shifted-prime divisor problem: Σ_{p≤X} τ(p+a) (Titchmarsh) and its class-restricted version
connection: Titchmarsh divisor problem counts divisors of p+a on average ↔ ES's divisor form 'd | 4Cp+1 in class' averaged over p is Titchmarsh with congruence; pointwise is the problem.
why: Bombieri–Friedlander–Iwaniec beyond-1/2 level for Titchmarsh may improve exceptional set exponents.
first_step: Check whether BFI-type level-of-distribution > 1/2 for fixed residue a applies to (4Cp+1) with class condition on divisors; estimate effect on 3/4 exponent.

title: Bilinear Kloosterman sums (Kowalski–Michel–Sawin) at prime modulus
connection: KMS bounded bilinear sums of Kloosterman sums beyond Pólya–Vinogradov range ↔ ES certificate counting via Kloosterman-type expansions at modulus related to p.
why: Bilinear Kloosterman bounds give pointwise-at-p cancellation in short ranges; could improve M_BM lower bound constant or the error in T(p).
first_step: Express T(p) or R(p)'s fluctuation via sums over modulus-p objects; check if KMS short-range bilinear bounds apply.

title: Short character sums with multiplicative structure: T(p) over hyperbolic region uB ≤ p
connection: T(p) = Σ_{uB ≤ ~p/4} (−uB/p)/φ(4uB) is a character sum over a hyperbola ↔ sums Σ_{n≤N} χ(n)τ(n) (character twisted divisor sums) have better-than-PV bounds.
why: Hyperbola character sums factor (χ(u)χ(B)), giving Dirichlet-hyperbola-method square-root-scale bounds; improving T(p) bound improves M_BM constant toward M₀.
first_step: Compute T(p)/M₀(p) for primes ≤ 10⁷ and check the empirical max; if bounded away from 1, try to prove |T| ≤ (1−δ)M₀ using L(1,χ) positivity.

title: Positivity via L(1,χ) > 0 and Siegel: T(p) as a smoothed L(1,χ_p)²-like object
connection: Σ_{u,B} χ(u)χ(B)/φ(4uB) ≈ L(1,χ)²·(local factors) ↔ T(p)'s main contribution might be L(1,χ_{−4})-twisted L(1,(·/p))² which is positive.
why: If T(p) ≈ c·L(1,χ)² log-terms with positive c, then M₀ − T is controlled by the size of L(1,χ) which is ≪ log p; giving the log² main term more cleanly.
first_step: Derive the asymptotic of T(p) in terms of L(1,(−4·/p))-type values via Mellin inversion; test numerically.

title: Dirichlet hyperbola method for R(p) with exact error tracking
connection: R(p) = Σ_C #{d | 4Cp+1 : d ≡ −1 mod 4C} ↔ split d ≤ √ and d > √; symmetry d ↔ (4Cp+1)/d preserves class (since product ≡ 1 mod 4C ⇒ cofactor ≡ −1).
why: Already used (R even). Exploit further: the pairing is an involution with no fixed points (squares excluded) — parity of half-count R/2 has no forced value (EVIDENCE fair coin). Record as done.
first_step: Check whether a refined involution (e.g. using d ↔ (4C'p+1)/d across different C) produces a fixed-point-only-at-squares structure.

title: Selberg's Λ² upper-bound sieve inverted: lower bound for 'not all events fail' via Turán sieve
connection: Turán sieve gives lower bounds for counts of objects hitting at least one condition from variance ↔ R(p) pointwise needs variance over a p-family — no family at fixed p, but family over (u,C) trials.
why: Turán-type inequality at fixed p: #{success} ≥ (Σ P)²/(Σ_{i,j} P_ij) in a probabilistic model over trials; but the 'probability' at fixed p is deterministic. Identify a randomisation at fixed p (e.g. random auxiliary prime) that preserves certificates.
first_step: Search for an auxiliary random variable at fixed p (e.g. random multiplier λ with certificates for λp mapping back) — check if 4/p certificates can be transported from 4/(λp)-type statements.

title: Transport from multiples: ES(kp) solutions that descend to ES(p)
connection: Solutions for kp do not in general descend to p ↔ but for special k (e.g. k | some denominator pattern), descent works: 4/(kp) = … with k dividing all three denominators ⟹ 4/p.
why: Gives a thick family (all k) of related problems at fixed p; if solutions of 4/(kp) with k | gcd structure are forced for some k, ES(p) follows.
first_step: Compute, for hard p, solutions of 4/(kp) for k ≤ 50 and classify which ones descend; measure descent fraction.

title: m/(kp) family: ES(p) ⟸ (4k)/(kp) three-term solutions with k | x,y,z
connection: Generalising: 4/p = 4k/(kp); three-term representations of 4k/(kp) with all denominators divisible by k are exactly ES(p) solutions scaled — so no gain; but representations of (4k+j)/(kp) − j/(kp) mix.
why: Mostly a sanity item: shows trivial transports are tautological; identifies the non-tautological ones (where denominators share only part of k).
first_step: Characterise algebraically when a solution of 4/(kp) yields one of 4/p (gcd conditions) and enumerate non-trivial transports for k ≤ 12.

title: Rational points of bounded height on the ES fibre counted by circle method in 3 variables? (Not enough variables) → use delta method on 4uBC − u − B = p
connection: Heath-Brown delta method counts representations by forms in ≥ 3 variables ↔ 4uBC − u − B = p is a cubic in 3 variables (degenerate: linear in each).
why: Multilinear forms are amenable to the circle method with fewer variables because of their structure (e.g. Kloosterman refinement for xy − zw); R(p) ~ main term log² p might be derivable but error bounds are the issue.
first_step: Set up delta-method counting of 4uBC − u − B = p with smooth weights; compute the singular series and integral; compare with M₀.

title: Divisor function in arithmetic progressions to large moduli (Fouvry–Iwaniec, Heath-Brown τ₃) applied to Σ_C
connection: τ in APs with modulus beyond √x (via Kloosterman, Deshouillers–Iwaniec) ↔ divisors of 4Cp+1 in class mod 4C averaged over C.
why: Average over C at fixed p is a genuine one-variable average (not over p) — exactly the kind of thick average available at a single p. Level-of-distribution results for τ(n) in APs n ≡ a mod q with q ~ n^{2/3} might count Σ_C at fixed p!
first_step: Write Σ_{C ≤ X} #{d | 4Cp+1, d ≡ −1 mod 4C} as Σ_d Σ_C 1[4Cp ≡ −1 mod d, d ≡ −1 mod 4C]; the d-sum with C free: for each d, the C with d ≡ −1 mod 4C ⟺ 4C | d+1. So count pairs (d, C) with 4C | d+1 and d | 4Cp+1 — rewrite and see if it reduces to a count of p in residue classes mod d (averaged over d) — Bombieri–Vinogradov at a single p? Check.

title: Reverse the roles: for each modulus m = 4C, list p for which some d|4Cp+1 is ≡ −1 mod m — a 'dual sieve' table
connection: Duality between p and modulus ↔ the set S_C = {p : C-slice succeeds} is a union of residue classes mod d for d ≡ −1 mod 4C.
why: S_C is periodic only if bounded d; with unbounded d it's a 'multiplicative' set. ES ⟺ ∪_C S_C ⊇ primes. Studying S_C's density and correlations between S_C, S_{C'} is a sieve-dimension question.
first_step: Compute densities of S_C among primes ≤ 10⁷ for C ≤ 30 and correlation matrix corr(1_{S_C}, 1_{S_{C'}}); test near-independence.

title: Brun–Titchmarsh in reverse: lower bounds for primes p ≤ X with no certificate of size ≤ B
connection: Lower-bound sieve for primes avoiding certificate classes ↔ B1 shows infinitely many under Dickson; an unconditional lower bound count for evaders of polylog-size menus.
why: Shows how big the menu must be (as a function of p) for ES; an unconditional result 'there are primes needing certificates of size ≥ (log p)^A' would be new calibration (repo mentions Linnik-based upper side).
first_step: Apply a lower-bound sieve (Rosser–Iwaniec) to the set of primes avoiding all classes −u mod 4uC−1 for 4uC−1 ≤ B; compute dimension κ and see if positive lower bound holds for B ~ (log X)^A.

title: Maynard–Tao multidimensional sieve: many primes simultaneously evading or satisfying certificate conditions
connection: Maynard's sieve finds bounded gaps between primes in admissible tuples ↔ admissible tuples of p-tied linear forms (4Cp+1 for several C) being simultaneously prime would be ES-hostile (no small divisors).
why: Shows that infinitely many p have many 4Cp+1 simultaneously having few prime factors (Maynard gives several primes among k forms) — a partial unconditional 'hard prime' construction; quantifies stress on ES.
first_step: Apply Maynard to forms {4Cp+1 : C ≤ k} (admissible?) to show infinitely many p with ≥ m of them prime; compute m for k = 50.

title: When 4Cp+1 is prime, the C-slice of (★) fails; when is 4Cp+1 = q·r with q ≡ −1 mod 4C?
connection: Prime 4Cp+1 kills slice C; semiprimes succeed iff a factor ≡ −1 mod 4C ↔ quadratic-character-like conditions on factors.
why: Breaking R(p) by factorisation type of 4Cp+1 gives a clean probabilistic model: success probability of slice C ≈ Σ over factorisation types.
first_step: Tabulate, over C ≤ 100 and p ≤ 10⁶, the success rate of slice C conditioned on Ω(4Cp+1) = 2, 3, 4…

title: Chen's theorem analogue: 4Cp+1 is P₂ for some small C
connection: Chen-type: for each p, some 4Cp+1 with C ≤ polylog is a product of ≤ 2 primes? ↔ unproven at fixed p; Chen is about averages over p.
why: Calibration: shows even 'some 4Cp+1 has a specific factorisation shape' at fixed p is out of reach of sieves — ES needs such fixed-p statements.
first_step: Record as barrier-calibration: list fixed-p statements about {4Cp+1 : C ≤ (log p)^A} that are known (e.g. not all prime? trivially: some is divisible by 3) and the strongest such.

title: Trivially-forced divisibility at fixed p: 4Cp+1 ≡ 0 mod ℓ for C ≡ −(4p)^{-1} mod ℓ
connection: For each small prime ℓ, some C < ℓ gives ℓ | 4Cp+1 ↔ the divisor ℓ is in class −1 mod 4C only if ℓ ≡ −1 mod 4C — a 'self-levelled' small-prime certificate.
why: This is the cheapest structured certificate family (d = ℓ prime): ES(p) ⟸ ∃ ℓ prime, C | (ℓ+1)/4, ℓ | 4Cp+1. That's p ≡ −(4C)^{-1} mod ℓ — a residue condition mod ℓ for each divisor C of (ℓ+1)/4: density ≈ τ((ℓ+1)/4)/ℓ per ℓ, sum diverges like Σ τ/ℓ ~ log²: matches log² main term!
first_step: Compute the fraction of R(p) coming from d prime (vs composite) for p ≤ 10⁷; if prime d dominate, the problem is 'p in a union of residue classes mod primes ℓ' — classical sieve setting (B1/B2 still).

title: Prime-modulus certificate family as a covering-by-primes question (Erdős covering with prime moduli)
connection: From previous: ES ⟸ p ∈ ∪_ℓ ∪_{C | (ℓ+1)/4} {−(4C)^{-1} mod ℓ} ↔ covering the primes by residue classes mod distinct primes ℓ with τ((ℓ+1)/4) classes each.
why: Covering systems with distinct prime moduli cannot cover ℤ when Σ (#classes)/ℓ converges or by Hough-type results; here Σ τ((ℓ+1)/4)/ℓ diverges — so covering is not excluded by density; but CRT construction evades finite subsets (B1).
first_step: Formalise 'prime-modulus covering with τ((ℓ+1)/4) classes per ℓ' and check whether known results (Erdős, Simpson–Zeilberger on coverings with prime moduli?) exclude covering all integers (likely yes via CRT) — then all primes is a different question (record).

title: Least prime ℓ ≡ −1 mod 4C dividing 4Cp+1: Linnik-type problem for a single integer
connection: Smallest prime factor in a residue class of a specific integer ↔ Linnik's theorem is about primes in APs, not factors of a given number.
why: Formulates the core 'tied-modulus divisor event' as a 'least prime factor in a class' problem, clean for literature search.
first_step: Search for literature on 'prime factors in residue classes of a fixed integer' (e.g. 'prime divisors of shifted primes in arithmetic progressions', Moree).

title: Artin's primitive root conjecture-type heuristic for ES gate (−1 in subgroup generated by divisor classes)
connection: Artin: a is a primitive root mod p for a positive density of p (Hooley under GRH) ↔ ES: classes of prime factors generate a subgroup containing −1.
why: Hooley's GRH-proof technique (Kummer-extension splitting) handles 'subgroup generated by a fixed element' — ES's elements vary with p, but the structure (Chebotarev in Kummer fields) is the tool for 'is −1 in ⟨g⟩'.
first_step: Express '−1 ∈ ⟨g⟩ mod q' as: ord(g) even and g^{ord/2} = −1; check whether certificate primes behave like random elements w.r.t. this event.

title: Ternary divisor problem: R(p) as τ₃-like count of factorisations 4uBC − u − B = p
connection: R(p) counts restricted 'three-factor' decompositions ↔ τ₃(n) has mean (log n)²/2 — matches R's log² scale!
why: Natural to compare R(p) with τ₃ of a p-tied integer (e.g. τ₃(4p+…)); maybe R(p) = Σ over a bounded set of τ₃(N_i(p)) restricted to classes.
first_step: Compute correlation between R(p) and τ₃(p+1), τ₃(p+3), τ(…) etc. for p ≤ 10⁶.

title: Exact formula: R(p) = Σ_{C} (τ_{−1 mod 4C}(4Cp+1)) — compute generating Dirichlet series in p
connection: Treat R(n) for all odd n: D(s) = Σ R(n) n^{-s} ↔ analytic properties (poles at s=1 of order 3?) give mean values; Tauberian.
why: Mean value ≍ log² — consistent with triple pole; a factorisation D(s) = ζ(s)^? L(s,…) would expose structure.
first_step: Compute D(s) formally: Σ_{u,B,C} (4uBC − u − B)^{-s}; find its analytic continuation properties numerically or via Mellin–Barnes.

title: Multiplicative energy of the divisor set of 4Cp+1
connection: Additive/multiplicative energy of divisor sets ↔ structured sets cover subgroups faster.
why: Divisor sets have maximal multiplicative structure (they're 'cubes' {Π p_i^{e_i}}); covering results for 'generalised geometric progressions' in (ℤ/q)^× are precise.
first_step: Model divisors as a generalised GP with k generators; compute the minimal k for which such sets cover −1 mod q generically; compare with Ω(4Cp+1).

title: Subset products in (ℤ/q)^× of random elements: probability −1 is hit with k elements
connection: Random model: k random elements of (ℤ/q)^×, probability some subproduct = −1 ↔ ES slice success probability given Ω(4Cp+1) = k.
why: Exact probabilities (from group structure: needs −1 in generated subgroup and a subproduct, not just subgroup element) give a refined heuristic for R(p) zero probability.
first_step: Compute exactly for q = 4C ≤ 200, k ≤ 6 the probability that subset products of k uniform elements include −1 (with constraint product of all ≡ −1·something?).

title: Hidden constraint: the product of all prime factors of 4Cp+1 is ≡ 1 mod 4C — subproduct ≡ −1 ⟺ complementary subproduct ≡ −1
connection: Since 4Cp+1 ≡ 1 mod 4C, d ≡ −1 ⟺ N/d ≡ −1: symmetric ↔ random-model must condition on total product ≡ 1.
why: Getting the conditioning right changes the predicted zero probability (repo's evenness). Sanity for all random models above.
first_step: Incorporate total-product conditioning into the subset-product model of the previous item and recompute probabilities.

title: Type I via p² + 4c²d: sums of two squares structure
connection: Type I: f | p² + 4c²d with f ≡ −p mod 4cd ↔ for d = 1, p² + 4c² = p² + (2c)² is a sum of two squares; its divisors are norms from ℤ[i].
why: Gaussian-integer factorisation of p² + (2c)² = (p + 2ci)(p − 2ci) gives divisors as norms of Gaussian divisors; class conditions become conditions on Gaussian primes — maybe a Hecke-character formulation (quartic).
first_step: For d = 1, express the condition f ≡ −p mod 4c for f | p²+4c² via Gaussian divisors α | p+2ci; check if the condition is a Hecke character (Größencharakter) condition on α.

title: Type I d=1 slice as Gaussian lattice-point problem: α | p + 2ci with N(α) ≡ −p mod 4c
connection: Continuing: ES Type I d=1 ⟺ ∃ c, α ∈ ℤ[i] with α | p + 2ci and N(α) ≡ −p mod 4c ↔ distribution of Gaussian divisors of a linear family p + 2ci in c.
why: The family {p + 2ci : c ≥ 1} is a vertical line in ℤ[i]; divisors of Gaussian integers on a line — like 'divisors of a + bi along b' — a 2D analogue of 4Cp+1 with more symmetry (Gaussian units, conjugation).
first_step: Numerically compute success rates for this slice and compare with Type II slices; test whether the conjugate pair (α, ᾱ) gives an involution with fixed points at squares.

title: Eisenstein integers and 4/p: a slice where p = a² + 3b² helps
connection: Primes p ≡ 1 mod 3 split in ℤ[ω] (all hard primes do, being ≡ 1 mod 840) ↔ a certificate built from p's ℤ[ω]-factorisation.
why: Hard primes split completely in many small fields; their factorisations π·π̄ are canonical objects at p (thick? no, but rigid). A certificate formula in terms of (a,b) with p = a² + 3b² would be an R-type identity on a non-residue-class set — not excluded by Mordell–Schinzel.
first_step: For hard primes p ≤ 10⁶, compute (a,b) with p = a²+3b², a²+b² representation, a²+2b², a²+5b²… and search for linear/quadratic expressions in a,b that give ES certificates for all p.

title: Identities in terms of sum-of-two-squares representation p = a² + b²
connection: Every p ≡ 1 mod 4 is a² + b² ↔ search for x,y,z polynomial in (a,b) with 4/(a²+b²) = 1/x+1/y+1/z holding identically or on an explicit infinite set.
why: Mordell–Schinzel forbids polynomial identities in n on residue classes containing squares, but identities in (a,b) are a different object: n = a²+b² is a polynomial in two variables. Does the obstruction persist? (Probably yes via specialisation b=0 giving squares a² — T1 obstruction! then need identities that avoid b = 0 ... record.)
first_step: Check: any identity in (a,b) specialises at b=0 to n = a² (odd square) where Type I/II solutions don't exist (T1) — so any (a,b)-identity must produce non-Type-I/II or fail at b = 0 — test whether rational functions with a pole at b = 0 escape this.

title: Identities with poles at the T1 locus: rational (not polynomial) parametrisations x(a,b) with denominators vanishing on b = 0
connection: Following the T1 specialisation obstruction: any (a,b)-identity must break at squares; rational functions with b in denominators break exactly there.
why: Integrality then requires b | numerators — a divisibility condition in (a,b) that may hold for all p via a choice among the many representations a² + b² (only one up to sign for primes!) — so only finitely many choices; record as likely-dead but clean test.
first_step: Search rational functions of low degree in (a,b) with denominators b^k for identities 4/(a²+b²) = Σ 1/x_i; then test integrality on primes.

title: Quaternion / sums of four squares representations: many representations (r₄(p) = 8(p+1)) as thick object
connection: p = a²+b²+c²+d² has 8(p+1) representations — a thick object at p ↔ certificate extraction from some representation.
why: Thick object × extraction rule (G1): we need a rule mapping some 4-square representation to an ES certificate; the thick set has size ≍ p, so a rule with success probability ≫ 1/p per rep suffices.
first_step: For p ≤ 10⁴, enumerate four-square representations and test simple formulas (e.g. x = (a²+b²)·k...) for producing certificates; record any rule with high success.

title: Three squares: p = a² + b² + c² representations (r₃ ≍ √p h) as thick object
connection: Odd p ≢ 7 mod 8 are sums of three squares with ≍ √p·L(1,χ) reps ↔ extraction rule to ES certificate.
why: Same G1 logic with an object of size √p tied to class numbers.
first_step: For hard p, enumerate three-square reps and search for any polynomial map (a,b,c) ↦ (x,y,z) yielding certificates on ≥ 1 rep for all p ≤ 10⁴.

title: Binary quadratic forms of discriminant −4p·k: reduced forms as thick objects (class number h(−4pk) ≈ √p)
connection: Reduced forms (a,b,c) with b² − 4ac = −4pk are ≍ √p in number ↔ ES certificate from a form whose coefficients satisfy a congruence.
why: Type II: 4uBC − u − B = p resembles forms with ac − b²-type relations; a bijection between certificates and special reduced forms would place ES inside class-group combinatorics (where Gauss genus theory and Cohen–Lenstra live).
first_step: Search for (k, map) such that each ES Type II certificate gives a reduced form of discriminant −4pk with a ≡ … ; enumerate for p ≤ 10³.

title: Cohen–Lenstra heuristics for 'class gate' events
connection: Probability a random abelian group has given structure ↔ (ℤ/4C)^× subgroup generated by divisor classes containing −1.
why: Mostly a modelling tool; could predict which C slices fail more often (those with large 2-rank of (ℤ/4C)^×).
first_step: Compute slice failure rate vs 2-rank of (ℤ/4C)^× for C ≤ 200 over many p.

title: 2-rank / Rédei symbols: 2-part of class groups and the −1-class event
connection: Is −1 a product of classes of prime factors: −1 is a 'genus character' object; Rédei matrices compute 4-ranks via Legendre symbols ↔ ES gate may be a Rédei-type matrix condition.
why: Smith's work on 4-ranks (Alexander Smith 2017, distribution of 2^∞ Selmer/class groups) handles exactly such Legendre-symbol matrices statistically.
first_step: Express 'some subproduct of primes q_i ≡ −1 mod 4C' using characters of (ℤ/4C)^× of 2-power order: a linear algebra condition over F_2 on (χ(q_i)) — compute the F_2 matrix for hard p.

title: F₂-linear-algebra reformulation of the 2-part of the class gate
connection: For C with (ℤ/4C)^× an elementary 2-group (C | 6), subproduct ≡ −1 is a linear system over F₂ ↔ exact solvability criterion via rank.
why: Gives an exact decision rule for small-C slices in terms of Legendre/Kronecker symbols of prime factors — a 'Rédei matrix' of p-tied integers.
first_step: For C = 1, 2, 3, 6 (where 4C ∈ {4,8,12,24}), write the condition as F₂-linear system on characters of prime factors of 4Cp+1; verify on data.

title: Covering by quadratic-character conditions: ES(p) ⟸ some explicit Legendre-symbol pattern of p
connection: F_q forcing lines ((q/p) = −1 ⟹ ES(p)) known for q ∈ {3,5,7} ↔ multi-symbol patterns (e.g. (3/p)=(5/p)=…=1 ⟹ ?).
why: Hard primes have all small q as QRs; question is the joint distribution; a theorem 'ES(p) if p is a QNR mod some q ≤ Q' + Burgess-like least-QNR bound p^{small} doesn't finish but an explicit 'all q ≤ 13 QR' class is where difficulty concentrates.
first_step: From repo EXSET_CHAR_FORCING.md, list proven forcing lines; compute fraction of primes ≤ 10⁹ not covered by them as a function of n₂(p).

title: Vinogradov's least-QNR conjecture and ES: n₂(p) ≪ p^ε ⟹ anything?
connection: If ES(p) followed from (q/p) = −1 for every prime q (all forcing lines), then n₂(p) finite would give ES — but forcing lines are open from q = 11.
why: Concrete target: prove F₁₁; any proof of F_q for all q would prove ES (since every prime p has some QNR q < p). Clean reduction worth recording explicitly.
first_step: Write the implication chain: (∀q prime: F_q) ⟹ ES; check if F_q for q ≤ n₂ bound under GRH (2 log² p) suffices — yes: then ES ⟸ (GRH ∧ ∀q ≤ 2log²p: F_q).

title: Quadratic reciprocity orientation: F_q is about (q/p); flip to (p/q) and use CRT-based identities
connection: (q/p) = (p/q) for p ≡ 1 mod 4 ↔ F_q becomes a condition on p mod q: p is a QNR mod q ⟹ ES(p). That's a residue-class condition mod q — so F_q is a finite covering statement mod q!
why: Since hard primes are ≡ 1 mod 4, F_q is a union of (q−1)/2 residue classes mod q; Mordell-style identities on these classes would prove F_q — but repo says F₁₁ open with a sterile point; so the classes are not covered by ET identities mod 11·(…). Check sterile point mechanism.
first_step: Read EXSET_CHAR_FORCING.md §7 on x** and determine which QNR classes mod 11 lack an ET identity at all moduli 11·M.

title: Sterile points as profinite objects: x** in Ẑ where all ET identities fail
connection: A sterile point is a profinite integer (point of Ẑ) where no ET identity class contains it ↔ compactness: if no sterile prime-like points exist in the closure of primes in Ẑ, ES would follow from finitely many identities — contradicting B1 — so sterile points must exist; their structure is the obstruction.
why: Classifying sterile profinite points (are they all squares in Ẑ? i.e. locally squares everywhere) would connect B1 to T1: sterile ⟺ 'locally a square' would be a clean theorem.
first_step: Test: are all known sterile points squares in ℤ_ℓ for every ℓ checked? Compute for x** its square-class in ℤ_ℓ for ℓ ≤ 50.

title: Compactness argument: ES holds for all n iff a certain closed subset of Ẑ contains no positive integers
connection: The set of n ∈ Ẑ not covered by ET identities is closed ↔ positive integers in it must be handled by non-identity (non-local) certificates.
why: Formalising this would define the 'global part' of ES precisely as integers in a profinite closed set (squares in Ẑ are in it). Then ES ⟺ integer points of that set (non-squares) each have a large certificate.
first_step: Define precisely: K = Ẑ minus ∪(open ET identity classes). Compute K ∩ (ℤ/M) projections for M up to 10⁶; check whether K equals the closure of squares or is larger.

title: Ultraproduct / nonstandard primes: a nonstandard counterexample p* in an ultrapower
connection: If ES is true, it's true in all models of PA where it's provable; a nonstandard model with ES failing at a nonstandard p* would show independence from weaker systems.
why: Model-theoretic view: properties of p* (e.g. p* ≡ square mod every standard m ⟹ p* a 'locally square' prime) mirror sterile points; a structural link between nonstandard counterexamples and profinite sterile points.
first_step: Write: p* nonstandard with no standard-size certificate ⟺ p* ∈ K (sterile set) for all standard moduli ⟹ p* is locally a square at all standard primes? Check logically.

title: Overspill: if every prime ≤ N has a certificate of size ≤ (log p)^A, by overspill some nonstandard N too — useless direction; reverse: underspill for counterexamples
connection: Overspill/underspill principles ↔ bounding certificate size uniformly.
why: Mostly logical hygiene: shows 'uniform polylog bound' and 'ES' are equivalent in nonstandard terms only with explicit bounds.
first_step: Skip unless pursuing logic angle; first step: write a paragraph mapping ES's bounded-quantifier form to overspill.

title: Shifted-square obstruction: why squares fail Type I/II via Jacobi symbols, and 'almost squares' (p = m² + small) as stress tests
connection: T1 kills odd squares; primes p = m² + k for small k are 'close to squares' ↔ maybe low certificate counts for small k.
why: If R(m² + k)/M is systematically small for small k, T1's influence leaks to neighbours — a quantitative T1 continuity phenomenon to explain or exploit.
first_step: Compute R(p)/M_BM(p) for primes p = m² + k, k ∈ {4, 16, 36, …} (to keep p ≡ 1 mod 4) vs random p; m ≤ 10⁴.

title: Primes of the form m² + 4 (Landau-type) and ES certificate counts
connection: p = m² + 4: Type II analysis with u, B small — p + u divisible by 4uC − 1 relates to m² + 4 + u factoring.
why: Polynomial families let algebra help: m² + 4 + u factors over ℤ[i] — maybe forced certificates (like 4X⁴ + 1 Sophie Germain).
first_step: Try to prove ES for all n = m² + 4 (odd m) via algebraic factorisation identities, analogous to repo's 4^s + k families.

title: ES for all n = 4m² + 1 / m² + 1-type families via Gaussian factorisation
connection: Polynomial values n = f(m) where f has algebraic structure (norm forms) ↔ thin-family proofs à la repo (J)62–(J)80.
why: Each such family that admits a proof is a new PROVED thin family; families with no finite ET covering need a moving window (repo technique).
first_step: Pick f(m) = m² + 1 (odd values?) or 4m² + 1; check if a finite ET covering exists (compute coverage mod M for growing M); if not, try window technique.

title: Bateman–Horn densities for primes in hard families as test of B1-type evasion
connection: Bateman–Horn predicts counts of primes in polynomial families ↔ quantify how many primes in a family each certificate class covers.
why: Calibration for which polynomial families are ES-hardest.
first_step: For families f(m) = am² + bm + c generating primes ≡ 1 mod 840, compute average R(f(m))/M; find hardest family.

title: Odd-square neighbours in the ES₅ word form: tuv − u − v = m² has no 'interior' words? T1 in word language
connection: ES₅ word certificates should exhibit T1 at squares ↔ word-level proof of T1 might identify an invariant (like a Jacobi symbol of t,u,v) that is constant on words.
why: An invariant constant on words but nonconstant on primes would be a hidden conservation law; T1 says it takes a forbidden value on squares.
first_step: Compute the Jacobi symbol combinations (t/·), (u/v)… on all ES₅ words for small n; look for a combination that equals 1 on all words of non-square n... (check repo first).

title: I3 extremal function: least u over primes, as a 'Jacobsthal function' analogue
connection: Least certifying interior endpoint u(p) ≤ 39 to 10⁹ ↔ Jacobsthal function j(m) (max gap in integers coprime to m) controls CRT evasions.
why: Jacobsthal bounds (Iwaniec: j(m) ≪ (log m)²) are pointwise results on CRT-evasion lengths — exactly the B1 cost question; growth of max u(p) should be compared with Jacobsthal-type predictions.
first_step: Model: to evade u ≤ U requires p avoiding certain classes mod moduli depending on u; compute the 'Jacobsthal-type' minimal evader size and compare with observed max u = 39 at 10⁹.

title: Iwaniec's Jacobsthal bound technique applied to certificate evasion
connection: Iwaniec proved j(m) ≪ (log m)² via sieve ↔ the evasion of certificate classes is a sieve with moduli 4uC−1; can a Jacobsthal-type upper bound show 'every p has a certificate with u ≤ (log p)^2'? No — p is fixed, not a free interval… but the trial variable u is an interval!
why: At fixed p, the variable u ranges over an interval [1, U]; ES Type II with fixed C... the conditions on u are 'u ≡ −p mod (4uC−1)' — modulus depends on u (tied), so not a Jacobsthal sieve. However I3 with t fixed: tuv − u − v = p ⟺ (tu−1)(tv−1) = tp + 1 — a divisor problem of tp+1 for each t. Record the precise mismatch.
first_step: Write the exact obstruction: for Jacobsthal, residue classes are fixed and the variable runs over an interval; for ES, residue class depends on the variable. Search for change of variables making the class fixed (e.g. v as variable with u fixed: (tu−1) | tp+1+(tu−1)... ).

title: (tu−1)(tv−1) = tp + 1: I3 as a divisor-in-class problem for tp+1
connection: tuv − u − v = p ⟺ t²uv − tu − tv = tp ⟺ (tu−1)(tv−1) = tp + 1 ↔ need a divisor of tp+1 that is ≡ −1 mod t (and ≥ 2t−1).
why: This is the same tied-modulus shape as 4Cp+1 (t = 4C). Clean confirmation that I3 and (★) are the same event family; also shows t odd allowed in I3 (extra slices).
first_step: Verify the identity and compare I3 slice-by-t success with (★) slices; list t values that are not ≡ 0 mod 4 and their contribution (they need the coordinate condition 4ℤ ∪ 8ℤ−p elsewhere).

title: Sum over t of #{d | tp+1, d ≡ −1 mod t}: the full I3 count as a thick object with t up to p
connection: Allowing t up to ~p gives a sum of ~p log p events; for t > √p, the divisor condition is about tp+1 having a divisor in a class mod t > √(tp) — Lenstra regime (≤ bounded count, decidable fast).
why: In the large-t regime, the condition d ≡ −1 mod t with d | tp+1 forces d small multiple structure: d = kt − 1 with (kt−1) | tp+1 ⟺ (kt−1) | (p + k)·t − (kt−1)·… ⟹ (kt − 1) | p + k: back to Type II trial form. Symmetry u ↔ k — consistent.
first_step: Map the I3 large-t regime onto small-k Type II trials explicitly; confirm the count identity numerically.

title: One-parameter form: R(p) = #{m ≡ 3 (mod 4) : r_p(m) | (m+1)/4}, r_p(m) = (−p mod m) (CHECKED p ≤ 1009)
connection: Trial form (4uC−1) | p+u with m = 4uC−1 forces u = r_p(m) (as 1 ≤ u < m), so R(p) counts moduli m ≡ 3 mod 4 whose ceiling-remainder divides (m+1)/4 ↔ a single-variable search over m.
why: A one-variable reformulation makes 'remainder of one integer modulo a running modulus' the whole problem — the classical object of the Dirichlet divisor problem and of p mod m statistics (Vinogradov), possibly opening Voronoi/exponential-sum tools.
first_step: Verified numerically (scripts/z52b_free_opus_check1.py, p ≤ 1009 incl. 409 → 0). Next: plot r_p(m)/m against m for hard p and study the arcs where r_p(m) is small (m just above p/q).

title: Piecewise-linear structure of r_p(m) = qm − p on ⌈p/m⌉ = q recovers the (u,B) symmetry
connection: On the piece ⌈p/m⌉ = q, r = qm − p and (qm−p) | (m+1)/4 implies r | p + q: the piece index q is B and r is u ↔ the pair-form symmetry u ↔ B.
why: Confirms there is no hidden extra structure in the one-parameter form, but gives an O(√p)-pieces description useful for Voronoi-type summation (sum over pieces of a divisibility of a linear function).
first_step: Write R(p) = Σ_q #{m in piece q : (qm − p) | (m+1)/4} and attempt van der Corput/Voronoi on the piece sums for small q (where pieces are long).

title: Shift form: R(p) = Σ_{B≥1} #{s | p+B : s ≡ −1 (mod 4B)} (CHECKED p ≤ 1009)
connection: From p + B = u(4BC − 1): ES-(★) ⟺ some shifted prime p + B has a divisor ≡ −1 modulo 4B ↔ divisors of consecutive integers above p, each with its own tied modulus.
why: Shows the B-variable and C-variable divisor forms (4Cp+1 vs p+B) are two faces; the shift form lives on an interval of integers above p where Erdős–Selfridge/consecutive-integer rigidity tools act, though the modulus 4B is still tied to the shift.
first_step: Verified numerically (scripts/z52b_free_opus_check1.py). Next: compute which B contribute for hard primes (are certificates concentrated at B small, i.e. on p+1, p+2, …?).

title: Consecutive-integer rigidity on (p, p+Q]: can a block of integers avoid all divisors ≡ −1 mod 4(n−p)?
connection: Shift form asks whether every block p+1..p+Q contains n with a divisor ≡ −1 mod 4(n−p) ↔ Erdős–Selfridge/Sylvester–Schur-type theorems on prime factors of consecutive integers are pointwise.
why: The catch (recorded): each n needs a divisor in a class tied to its own offset, so CRT can make p+B avoid it for B ≤ Q (B1); but for B ~ √p the condition becomes 'n = p+B has a divisor ≡ −1 mod 4B in [4B−1, ...]', i.e. a factorisation near-square — Sylvester–Schur-type large-prime-factor results could interact.
first_step: Compute for hard p the distribution of contributing B (as fraction of √p); if many come from B ≍ √p, study whether 'consecutive integers near p have near-square factorisations with prescribed class' has literature (search 'divisors close to square root of consecutive integers').
