title: Additive bases: is the set of 'certificate-friendly' integers an additive basis of finite order?
connection: Define A = {n : ES(n) has a certificate of a simple type}; additive basis results (Schnirelmann) ↔ multiplicative closure of ES (if ES(a) then ES(ka)).
why: ES set is multiplicatively closed upward (multiples); it's a 'multiplicative ideal-like' set — primitive elements are the problem. Primitive sets theory (Erdős primitive set conjecture proved by Lichtman) might apply to 'minimal ES-failures'.
first_step: Note: the set of n failing ES (if any) is closed under taking divisors >1? (If ES(d) then ES(n) for d|n, so failures' divisors fail.) So failures form a divisor-closed set ⊂ primes∪{1}-generated: only primes. Record the clean fact and think about primitive-set density bounds (Lichtman).

title: Erdős primitive set conjecture (Lichtman 2022) as structure for failures of related numerator problems
connection: For m/n problems with exceptions (m = 8), the minimal exceptions form a primitive set ↔ Σ 1/(n log n) ≤ that of primes (Lichtman).
why: For m ≥ 5 exceptions, primitive-set bounds constrain how exceptions are distributed; tells whether exceptions are 'prime-like'.
first_step: List minimal 8/n exceptions ≤ 10⁶ and compute Σ 1/(n log n); compare with primes' value.

title: Geometry: ES as a lattice point on a hyperboloid-like surface in 3D and Minkowski–Hlawka counts
connection: Positive solutions (x,y,z) lie on a smooth surface in ℝ³ (cubic) ↔ counting lattice points on surfaces near the asymptotic directions (where one coordinate dominates).
why: Lattice points on curved surfaces: counts ≍ area / curvature-weighted; ES surface's curvature degenerates at infinity — where solutions concentrate.
first_step: Compute the 'area' of the ES surface patch in the box [p/4, p²]³ weighted appropriately and compare with log² p — a geometric derivation of the main term.

title: Convex geometry: the region of trial pairs as a hyperbolic region and its lattice width
connection: Hyperbolic regions {uB ≤ X} have small 'flatness' (Khinchine flatness theorem) ↔ certificates are lattice points in a coset lattice intersected with this region.
why: Flatness theorem: a convex body with no lattice points has small lattice width — but the hyperbolic region isn't convex; however, its convex pieces (u ≤ U, B ≤ V boxes) are.
first_step: For a fixed (u,C) box, the certificate set is a coset of a lattice of determinant ~ uC; apply flatness to decide when a box must contain a coset point (it must if box is large relative to modulus) — computes 'guaranteed' boxes and shows the tied-modulus problem.

title: Algebraic combinatorics: q-analogue of ES (q-integers [n]_q) and its solvability
connection: Replace n by [n]_q = 1 + q + … + q^{n−1}: 4/[n]_q = Σ 1/[x_i]_q in ℚ(q)? ↔ q-deformations sometimes make problems rigid.
why: If a q-analogue has polynomial-identity solutions, specialising q → 1 might give ES; Mordell–Schinzel suggests obstruction persists, but the q-world has extra freedom (cyclotomic factorisations of [n]_q).
first_step: Search for solutions of 4/[p]_q = 1/A(q) + 1/B(q) + 1/C(q) with A,B,C ∈ ℤ[q] for small primes p via polynomial factorisation of [p]_q-related expressions.

title: Polynomial ES over ℤ[T] (not F_q[T]): 4/f(T) = Σ 1/g_i(T) and specialisation
connection: Solutions in ℤ[T] for polynomial n(T) give identity families ↔ Mordell–Schinzel classification.
why: Systematic: for each polynomial n(T) of degree ≤ 2, decide existence of ℤ[T] solutions; the set of n(T) admitting them maps to proved thin families.
first_step: Enumerate quadratic n(T) = aT² + bT + c with small coefficients and search ℤ[T] solutions with degree ≤ 4 denominators.

title: Model theory of (ℤ, +, |, ≡): decidability of fragments containing ES-like statements
connection: Presburger arithmetic with divisibility (Bel'tyukov, Lipshitz) is decidable for existential sentences ↔ ES(n) for fixed n is existential with divisibility.
why: Lipshitz's decidability of existential theory of (ℤ, +, |) gives an algorithm deciding ES(p) for fixed p without bounding variables — curiosity; its algorithm may expose a structural 'reason' (local-global for divisibility systems).
first_step: Read Lipshitz 'The Diophantine problem for addition and divisibility' and check whether ES(p) (with xyz multiplication eliminated via Type II linearisation) fits into the decidable fragment — and what the decision procedure's 'local-global' principle says.

title: Local-global principle for systems of linear divisibilities (Lipshitz/Bel'tyukov)
connection: Existential (ℤ,+,|) theory satisfies a local-global principle: a system of divisibilities among linear forms is solvable iff solvable mod all primes powers (with conditions) ↔ ES Type II: (4uC − 1) | p + u is a divisibility between non-linear forms; but u fixed gives linear in C.
why: If ES (or a sufficient condition) could be phrased as a system of linear divisibilities with finitely many unknowns, a local-global principle would decide it — and locally ES is always solvable!
first_step: Find: with u fixed as a parameter, is '∃C: (4uC − 1) | p + u' a linear divisibility system? It is: ∃C,k: k(4uC − 1) = p + u — non-linear (kC). Search for a linear-divisibility sufficient condition, e.g. '∃C: (4C − 1) | (p + 1)' (u=1): linear in C! Then local-global says solvable iff locally solvable — but local solvability of 4C − 1 | p + 1 as C varies ⟺ p+1 has a divisor ≡ 3 mod 4 … check the theorem's precise statement (it may need the divisor to be a linear form in the variables on both sides).

title: Hilbert's 10th problem over ℤ with divisibility: Diophantine definability of 'has a divisor ≡ −1 mod m'
connection: The predicate D(N,m) = ∃d | N, d ≡ −1 mod m is existential ↔ complexity of deciding ES-type predicates.
why: Logical classification only; supports TFNP items.
first_step: Note D(N,m) is in NP (certificate d) and coNP? (unknown); state as complexity question.

title: Reverse mathematics: which subsystem proves ES for n ≤ N uniformly? (RCA₀ trivially) — and Π₁ conservativity
connection: ES is Π₁ (bounded search), hence if true it is provable in … only if provable; Π₁ statements provable in ACA₀ are provable in PA (conservativity).
why: Clarifies that strong set-theoretic methods give no extra power for ES beyond PA (modulo conservativity), so analytic proofs via ACA₀-formalisable tools are 'allowed'.
first_step: Write one paragraph documenting the logical strength landscape (ES ∈ Π₁; conservativity of ACA₀/WKL₀ over PA/IΣ₁ for Π₁ statements).

title: Analogy: Fermat's last theorem via modularity — is there a 'Frey object' for an ES counterexample?
connection: FLT: hypothetical counterexample ↦ Frey curve with impossible properties ↔ ES counterexample p ↦ object (curve, Galois rep, form) whose properties are forced to be impossible.
why: Contradiction-from-counterexample is R-type rigidity; a 'Frey object' for ES would need to encode 'all certificates fail' — a highly non-local condition, unlike FLT's equation.
first_step: Brainstorm: given p with R(p)=0, list derived objects (e.g. the set of all 4Cp+1 have no divisor ≡ −1 mod 4C, so certain characters χ mod 4C satisfy Σ_{d|N} χ(d)χ(−1)… = 0) and check if any yields an L-function with forced zeros.

title: Character-sum identity for a failing slice: Σ_{χ mod 4C} χ(−1) Σ_{d | N} χ(d) = 0
connection: Slice C fails ⟺ #{d | N : d ≡ −1 mod 4C} = (1/φ(4C)) Σ_χ χ(−1)·Σ_{d|N} χ(d) = 0 ↔ Σ_{d|N}χ(d) = Π_{q^e ∥ N}(1 + χ(q) + … + χ(q)^e) is multiplicative.
why: Failure means a specific linear combination of multiplicative products vanishes for all C simultaneously — an exact algebraic condition; for many C at once it may be over-determined.
first_step: For a (★)-failing prime (409), compute these product vectors for C ≤ 20 and look at the structure of the vanishing (which characters contribute negative mass).

title: Polynomial Freiman–Ruzsa (Gowers–Green–Manners–Tao) and small-doubling sets of divisor classes
connection: PFR (proved 2023 over F₂ⁿ) gives structure for sets with small doubling ↔ divisor-class sets that avoid −1 have structure (contained in cosets).
why: If 'avoids −1 for all C' forces small-doubling structure across C, PFR-type inverse theorems might produce a contradiction.
first_step: Check: for (★)-failing primes, do divisor-class sets mod 4C have small doubling (|AA| ≤ K|A|)? Compute K.

title: Inverse theorem viewpoint: avoiding −1 forces the subproduct set into an index-2 subgroup coset structure
connection: Subset products avoiding −1 ↔ Kneser/inverse theorems (repo used Kneser at a failing window).
why: Already partially done (Kneser at forced window); generalise to all C simultaneously: −1 ∉ subproducts for every C — a family of inverse conditions on one integer family.
first_step: List, for (★)-failing primes, the index of the subgroup generated by prime factors of 4Cp+1 in (ℤ/4C)^× for C ≤ 50: is it always a subgroup not containing −1?

title: Ergodic Ramsey: multiple recurrence along p-tied sequences
connection: Furstenberg correspondence for statements about sets of integers ↔ ES is about one integer, not sets — weak fit.
why: Recorded as low-confidence: possible if one considers the set of failing primes and asks for structure (they can't contain APs? since ES failures can't fill an AP (PROVED in repo)).
first_step: Read the repo's proof that ES failures cannot fill an AP and ask whether a Szemerédi-type density statement for failures follows (failures have density 0 anyway).

title: Dimension theory: Hausdorff dimension of p-adic limits of failing primes (if infinitely many)
connection: If infinitely many (★)-failures existed, their closure in Ẑ is a compact set ↔ its dimension measures 'how sterile'.
why: Gives a quantitative profinite object for (★) failures (which are known to exist: 14 ≤ 10¹⁰); compare with sterile set K.
first_step: Compute residues of the 14 (★)-failing primes mod small moduli and see whether they lie in a small profinite set (e.g. all squares mod 3·5·7·…).

title: Hypergraph containers: number of 'certificate-free' prime configurations
connection: Container method counts independent sets in hypergraphs ↔ primes avoiding all certificate classes as independent sets of a hypergraph on residues.
why: Container lemma gives upper bounds on the number of 'evader' configurations — quantitative B1 sharpness.
first_step: Formulate the hypergraph whose edges are certificate classes; apply container counting to bound evaders up to X (heuristic).

title: Probabilistic method with alterations: random p-tied object then fix
connection: Erdős's alteration method ↔ choose random C, get N = 4Cp+1 with random factorisation; ES needs the class gate. Alteration: multiply/divide by small primes to fix the class? (not allowed: N is fixed).
why: Recorded as a check that the alteration freedom ES lacks is precisely 'modifying N'. The I3 form with t free gives N = tp+1 for all t — more freedom.
first_step: Compute success probability per t in I3 slices vs per C in (★); confirm the extra freedom quantitatively.

title: Hilbert's irreducibility with integral specialisations: non-thin sets of p where certificates exist
connection: Certificate-existence sets are unions of thin/non-thin sets ↔ Hilbert irreducibility ensures generic specialisations.
why: Abstract; flagged for an algebraic geometer.
first_step: Ask: is the set {p : C-slice succeeds} a thin set complement? (It's a union of residue classes mod variable d — non-thin.)

title: Teichmüller / mapping class group dynamics: SL₂(ℤ) words as Dehn twists on a torus
connection: SL₂(ℤ) = mapping class group of the torus; ES₅ words as products of Dehn twists ↔ curves on a torus with intersection numbers tied to p.
why: Geometric reformulation: ES(p) ⟺ some simple closed curves with prescribed intersection numbers exist — curve-complex combinatorics might give existence arguments.
first_step: Translate an ES₅ word [[a,p],[c,d]] into a pair of simple closed curves on the torus with intersection number p; examine the constraint 'c ∈ 4ℕ, a ≡ d ≡ −1 mod c' geometrically.

title: Hyperbolic 3-manifolds / Bianchi groups: ES over imaginary quadratic orders via SL₂(O_K) words
connection: Generalised SL₂ form over O_K ↔ ES_Q1 over ℤ[i] (repo) has failures; Bianchi group geometry may explain them.
why: Geometric explanation of the 6 Gaussian failures (e.g. via cusps of the Bianchi orbifold) would be a new structural fact for siblings.
first_step: For the six ES_Q1 failures (2+5i, 4+5i, …), compute their position relative to Bianchi group fundamental domain features (cusps, elliptic points).

title: Dessins d'enfants / Belyi maps: the ES surface's fibration branched over 3 points?
connection: If the map (x,y,z) ↦ n restricted to some curve is a Belyi map, Galois action on dessins might act on ES solution structure.
why: Speculative; Belyi maps tie combinatorics to Galois action.
first_step: Check whether the map from the curve {y = z} on ES surfaces to the n-line is branched over ≤ 3 points.

title: Combinatorics on words: the Christoffel word / Sturmian structure of continued fraction certificates
connection: Christoffel words encode rationals a/b and their CF ↔ ES₅ CF length ≤ 3 words.
why: Word combinatorics (palindromes, standard factorisation of Christoffel words) may produce a combinatorial proof of existence of a short factorisation.
first_step: Compute Christoffel words of 4/p and of certificate rationals; look for standard factorisations corresponding to ES solutions.

title: Kronecker's theorem / three-distance theorem for {p/m}
connection: Three-gap theorem for {nα} ↔ distribution of p mod m over m; hits are zeros of a remainder function.
why: Rigid structure of gaps sometimes forces hits; e.g. in ceiling-remainder form, r_p(m) takes values in structured arithmetic progressions on pieces.
first_step: On each piece q, r = qm − p runs through an AP with difference q; the target r | (m+1)/4 — test whether three-distance-type regularity forces hits on long pieces (small q).

title: Small-q pieces: B = q small ⟹ condition u | p + B with u ≡ −p mod B, i.e. divisors of p+1, p+2, … in classes
connection: For small B the C-equation reads: p + B has a divisor u ≡ … Actually p + B = u(4BC − 1) ⟹ the cofactor 4BC − 1 ≡ −1 mod 4B divides p + B ↔ the shift form at small B.
why: Small-B slices are 'divisors of p+B for B ≤ K in class −1 mod 4B': these are K concrete integers next to p. The union over B ≤ K gives a fixed menu (B1 applies), but how fast does coverage grow with K?
first_step: Compute fraction of primes ≤ 10⁸ covered by B ≤ K slices for K = 1..100; fit coverage curve.

title: B=1 slice of (★) ⟺ (p+1)/2 has a prime factor ≡ 3 (mod 4) — a Landau–Ramanujan event
connection: B = 1 slice: need divisor s ≡ −1 mod 4 of p + 1 with s ≥ 3 ↔ p + 1 = 2·odd; odd part has a divisor ≡ 3 mod 4 iff odd part has a prime factor ≡ 3 mod 4 … at an odd power? (product of primes ≡ 1 mod 4 gives ≡ 1).
why: Exact criterion: B=1 slice succeeds iff (p+1)/2 is not a product of primes ≡ 1 mod 4 (i.e. not a sum-of-two-squares-ish with only 1 mod 4 primes). Fails with density ~ c/√log p (Landau) — so B=1 alone handles all but a (log p)^{-1/2} fraction. Simple and illustrative.
first_step: CHECKED (scripts/z52b_free_opus_check2.py): criterion exact for all 8977 primes p ≡ 1 (4) below 2·10⁵; B=1 fails for 13.6% of them. Next: fit the failure fraction against c/√(log p) (Landau–Ramanujan) up to 10⁹.

title: Iterated Landau–Ramanujan: B-slice fails iff all prime factors of (p+B) avoid a set of classes mod 4B — a 'multiplicatively constrained' integer
connection: Generalising: slice B fails iff the subgroup/subset-product structure of prime factors of p+B avoids −1 mod 4B ↔ for B where (ℤ/4B)^× has a quadratic character separating −1, failure ⟸ all prime factors in its kernel: Landau–Ramanujan-type density (log)^{−1/2}.
why: Each slice fails with probability ~ (log p)^{−δ_B}; joint failure of K slices ~ product if independent — gives a clean heuristic exponent for 'K slices all fail' and connects to sieve dimension.
first_step: Compute δ_B (the density exponent of slice-failure) for B ≤ 30 theoretically (via Chebotarev in (ℤ/4B)^×) and compare with data.

title: Sieve of 'multiplicatively constrained' shifts: primes p with p+1, p+2, …, p+K all composed of primes in prescribed classes
connection: Simultaneous Landau–Ramanujan conditions on consecutive shifts p+B ↔ sieve of dimension Σ δ_B; such primes exist (heuristically) with density (log)^{−Σδ_B}.
why: Shows quantitatively how a (★)-failure is built: all small shifts must be 'class-constrained' integers. The 14 known failures could be checked against this mechanism.
first_step: For p = 409 and the other (★)-failures, factor p+B for B ≤ 50 and verify each is class-constrained mod 4B; identify the slowest-failing B.

title: Bounded gaps (Zhang–Maynard) technology for 'consecutive shifts all constrained' — upper bound on (★)-failures
connection: Upper-bound sieves for simultaneous multiplicative constraints on p+1,…,p+K ↔ #(★)-failures ≤ X ≪ X/(log X)^{1+Σδ_B} (heuristic upper bound becomes theorem via Selberg sieve).
why: A rigorous upper bound on (★)-failures (as a sieve upper bound) is achievable and new? It's an exceptional-set bound for (★) alone — compare with repo's ES exceptional set exponent (3/4); (★) alone can't beat Linnik-type phenomena but upper bound sieve is fine.
first_step: Write the Selberg upper-bound sieve for primes p ≤ X with p+B class-constrained for all B ≤ K and compute the resulting bound as K → ∞ with X.

title: Triangle geometry: 1/r = 1/r_a + 1/r_b + 1/r_c, so ES(n) ⟺ a triangle with inradius n/4 and integer exradii
connection: Classical identity 1/r = Σ 1/r_a (and s² = r_a r_b + r_b r_c + r_c r_a); any positive exradii determine a triangle ↔ ES solutions are exactly triangles with integral exradii and inradius n/4.
why: Imports triangle geometry (Heronian/rational triangles, integer-exradius literature) and gives a geometric invariant s² = e₂(x,y,z); the subfamily with s rational is 'Heronian-like' and may have its own parametrisation.
first_step: Verify the 'any positive exradii ⟹ triangle' claim; then compute, over ES solutions for p ≤ 10⁴, how often e₂(x,y,z) is a perfect square (rational semiperimeter) and search literature for 'integer exradii triangles'.

title: Triangle altitudes: 1/r = 1/h_a + 1/h_b + 1/h_c — ES as integer altitudes with inradius n/4
connection: Same reciprocal identity for altitudes ↔ ES solutions satisfying the triangle inequality on 1/h's are triangles with integer altitudes and inradius n/4.
why: Integer-altitude triangles are studied in recreational geometry; the triangle-inequality condition splits ES solutions into 'geometric' and 'non-geometric' ones — a new invariant to tabulate.
first_step: For p ≤ 10⁴, classify ES solutions by whether 1/x < 1/y + 1/z holds (altitude-realisable) and check if every p has a realisable one.

title: Sangaku (Japanese temple geometry) problems with unit-fraction radius relations
connection: Many sangaku give relations like 1/√r = Σ 1/√r_i or 1/r = Σ 1/r_i for tangent circles ↔ ES as an integer-radius configuration.
why: Curiosity/outreach; a configuration with 1/r = 1/r1 + 1/r2 + 1/r3 among mutually tangent circles might connect ES to Descartes/Apollonian integrality.
first_step: Search sangaku collections (Fukagawa–Rothman 'Sacred Mathematics') for a three-reciprocal radius relation and check if it's Descartes-compatible.

title: Cubic-with-integer-roots form: ES(n) ⟺ T³ − aT² + 4jT − nj has three positive integer roots for some a, j
connection: x,y,z are roots of T³ − e₁T² + e₂T − e₃ and 4e₃ = n·e₂ forces e₂ = 4j, e₃ = nj (up to gcd adjustments) ↔ splitting of a 2-parameter family of cubics over ℤ.
why: Turns ES into 'a specific 2-parameter cubic family has a totally split member' — Galois-group/Hilbert-irreducibility statistics and discriminant-square conditions apply; note f(n/4) = (n²/16)(n/4 − a).
first_step: Check the gcd bookkeeping (e₂ divisible by 4 when n odd?), then compute the discriminant of the family as a polynomial in (a,j,n) and test whether 'discriminant is a square' is a tractable curve condition.

title: Signed certificate counts with exact formulas (Jacobi-type): search for a sign ε(u,B,C) making Σ ε an explicit nonzero function
connection: r₂(n) = 4Σ_{d|n} χ₋₄(d) is a signed divisor count with an exact formula ↔ find ε on ES certificates so that S(p) = Σ ε is a class number, a divisor sum of p±k, or a Legendre-symbol expression that never vanishes.
why: If |S(p)| ≥ 1 is forced by an exact formula, R(p) ≥ 1 follows (|S| ≤ R) — the 'exact charge identity' column of G1, pointwise and without lower-tail estimates.
first_step: Compute, for p ≤ 10⁴, S_χ(p) = Σ over certificates of χ(u), χ(B), χ(C), χ(u+B) etc. for all characters χ mod ≤ 24; search each sequence in OEIS / fit to class numbers and divisor sums.

title: Witten-index analogue: a deformation-invariant signed count of certificates
connection: In physics an index (signed count of ground states) is invariant under deformations, so it can be computed at an easy point ↔ a signed ES count depending only on p mod M would be computable from small primes.
why: A deformation-invariant signed count nonzero on the hard classes would prove existence; T1 forces it to vanish at odd squares, which constrains the candidate (it must 'see' squareness, e.g. through Jacobi symbols).
first_step: Using the signed-count data from the previous item, test which signed sums S(p) are periodic in p (depend only on p mod M); any periodic nonzero one on all p ≡ 1 mod 840 classes is a candidate.

title: Categorification: R(p) as dim H⁰ of a complex whose Euler characteristic is explicit
connection: If certificates span H⁰ of a natural complex (e.g. Koszul complex of the divisibility conditions) with χ = explicit positive quantity and H¹ small, existence follows ↔ Euler-characteristic arguments in algebraic combinatorics.
why: Speculative but concrete: Euler characteristics are exact and often computable from local data — an R-type input.
first_step: Write the Koszul complex for the ideal (4uC − 1)·k − (p + u) over a polynomial ring truncated by degree bounds and compute its Euler characteristic numerically for small p.

title: Count congruences of R(p) modulo 3, 5, 8 and of partial counts R_C(p)
connection: G1 'count congruence' column: if R(p) ≢ 0 (mod m) for all p in some class, existence follows ↔ repo tested mod 2/mod 4 (fair coin).
why: Cheap scan of other moduli and of weighted/partial counts (restricted to C in a residue class, or to u ≡ B mod k) for a forced nonzero residue.
first_step: Compute R(p) and partial counts mod m for m ≤ 12 over primes p ≡ 1 mod 24 up to 10⁷; report any residue never taken (especially 0).

title: Ramanujan-sum expansion of the trial indicator: 1[m | N] = (1/m) Σ_{d|m} c_d(N)
connection: R(p) = Σ_{(u,C)} (1/m) Σ_{d|m} c_d(p+u) with m = 4uC−1 ↔ Ramanujan–Fourier expansion separates main term (d = 1) and oscillation (Ramanujan sums c_d(p+u)).
why: Ramanujan sums are explicit; regrouping by d gives R(p) = Σ_d (Σ_{m ≡ 0 (d)} …) c_d(·) — possibly revealing a d-level where cancellation fails exactly at squares (T1).
first_step: Compute the contribution of each d ≤ 100 to R(p) for hard p and for odd squares; see which d carry the T1 cancellation.

title: Siegel-zero world: what does an exceptional character imply for ES?
connection: Heath-Brown derived twin primes from Siegel zeros; Siegel-zero worlds make χ_D(q) = −1 for most small primes q ↔ ES F_q forcing lines need (q/p) = −1 for some proven q.
why: Conditional-on-Siegel-zero results are a legitimate 'illusory world' strategy; if exceptional χ_D forces many primes to be QNR-rich, F₃/F₅/F₇ lines cover more primes — check if it covers all.
first_step: Read Heath-Brown 'Prime twins and Siegel zeros' (1983) structure; formulate: under a Siegel zero for χ_D, are all large primes p with χ_D(p) = 1 forced into a forcing line? (likely not; record why).

title: Matrix Erdős–Straus: 4A⁻¹ = X⁻¹ + Y⁻¹ + Z⁻¹ over M₂(ℤ) with positivity
connection: Noncommutative sibling: replace integers by integer matrices (positive definite or positive entries) ↔ ES at A = pI or det A = p.
why: Matrix versions have more freedom (non-commutativity); if solvable by identity for all A with det A = p, a 'trace/determinant descent' might recover integer ES — or show where freedom is lost.
first_step: Search for solutions with X, Y, Z ∈ M₂(ℤ) symmetric positive definite for A = diag(p, 1) or companion matrices; record whether integer-matrix ES is always trivially solvable.

title: Signed ES (one negative denominator) as relaxation calibration
connection: 4/n = 1/x + 1/y − 1/z: check whether a polynomial identity solves all n ↔ positivity is the essential ES constraint.
why: If signed ES has identities on all classes, positivity is where Mordell–Schinzel bites; understanding how sign-flips evade T1 (they must) localises the obstruction to the positive cone.
first_step: Search for polynomial identities for 4/n = 1/x + 1/y − 1/z on all residue classes (e.g. via SMT templates); test at odd squares to see which T1 step a negative sign breaks.

title: Small-solution strengthening: ES with max(x,y,z) ≤ p·(log p)^A — when does it first fail?
connection: Strengthenings with size bounds ↔ certificates with small C (C ≤ polylog) correspond to small denominators.
why: Determines the 'natural size' of certificates; if a polylog-bounded version holds to 10⁹ with small A, it's a sharper conjecture with possible structure; if it fails, failures are informative.
first_step: For primes ≤ 10⁸, compute min over solutions of max(x,y,z)/p and record max over p; fit growth vs log p.

title: Restricted-denominator strengthening: one denominator a power of 2 times something
connection: ES with x ∈ {2^k·m : m ≤ M} ↔ like p + 2^k problems (Erdős: fails on APs).
why: A strengthening expected to fail (B1-style) gives cheap calibration of how much freedom ES needs.
first_step: Find the first prime ≡ 1 mod 24 for which no solution has x a power of 2 times a divisor of something small; tabulate.

title: Near-miss gap g(p) = min{4/p − (1/x+1/y+1/z) > 0} and its distribution
connection: Egyptian under-approximations ↔ ES ⟺ gap 0 attainable; the minimal positive gap measures how 'close' p is to failure in a continuous sense.
why: If hard primes have systematically larger minimal positive gaps, gap-based potential functions might guide search or reveal a continuous invariant.
first_step: Compute g(p)·p³ (or appropriately normalised) for primes ≤ 10⁵ restricted to small denominators; compare hard vs easy primes.

title: Four-term rescue size: minimal largest denominator when a 4th unit fraction is allowed to be huge
connection: 4/p = 1/x + 1/y + 1/z + 1/w with w forced large ↔ measures 'ES defect' at p.
why: Gives a continuous difficulty measure even when 3-term solutions are plentiful; correlations with R(p) test whether difficulty is one-dimensional.
first_step: For p ≤ 10⁵ compute the minimal max(x,y,z) such that the remainder 4/p − Σ is a unit fraction 1/w with w ≤ p³; compare with R(p).

title: First-term offset k: x = (p + 4k + 3)/4 and the binary remainder (4k+3)/(px)
connection: Choosing x = ⌈p/4⌉ + k leaves (4k+3)/(p·x) to be written as 2 unit fractions (Rav criterion: divisors d₁,d₂ of p·x with (4k+3) | d₁ + d₂) ↔ a 1-parameter family of binary problems.
why: Gives a simple 'search depth' measure k*(p); a bound k*(p) ≤ (log p)^A would be an ES-strength conjecture with a clean shape for probabilistic modelling (each k succeeds with probability ~ τ(px)/(4k+3)).
first_step: Compute k*(p) for primes ≤ 10⁸ and its max growth; model success probability per k via divisor counts of px.

title: Type I / Type II complementarity: are the primes where Type II is scarce rich in Type I?
connection: f_I(p) and f_II(p) counts ↔ correlation across primes.
why: Negative correlation would suggest a conservation-type law (a combined invariant), positive correlation suggests common difficulty driver (local factors).
first_step: Compute Spearman correlation of f_I(p)/log³p and f_II(p)/log³p over primes ≤ 10⁷ (repo data) after removing local-factor main terms.

title: Transport between nearby primes: 4/p = 4/q + 4(q−p)/(pq)
connection: If q close to p has a solution and the correction 4(q−p)/(pq) combines nicely ↔ continuity-type arguments (rare in arithmetic).
why: Likely dead (corrections need extra terms), but checking whether 'ES(q) + small structure ⟹ ES(p)' for q − p ∈ {4, 8, 12} ever works is cheap.
first_step: For p ≤ 10⁵, test whether some solution of 4/q (q = p+4k prime) shares two denominators with a solution of 4/p; record frequency.

title: Correlations R(p) vs R(p + 840k): local vs global difficulty
connection: Primes in the same class mod 840 share local data ↔ if R/M is strongly correlated for p, p + 840k, difficulty is local; if not, global randomness.
why: Quantifies the 'lottery' model; complements the ML feature-importance item.
first_step: Compute correlation of R(p)/M_BM(p) and R(p')/M_BM(p') for prime pairs with p' − p = 840k, k ≤ 100.

title: Shparlinski's modular-hyperbola survey as toolbox for the e-slice form
connection: Points on xy ≡ a (mod m) are well distributed (Kloosterman/Weil) ↔ e-slice: −1 ∈ {ab⁻¹ mod e : ab | N}.
why: The survey collects bounds for short boxes on modular hyperbolas — relevant if one restricts to divisors in short ranges.
first_step: Read Shparlinski, 'Modular hyperbolas' (arXiv:1103.2879; Jpn. J. Math. 2012) and list results about points with coordinates restricted to divisor sets.

title: Bernstein 1962 (Crelle) polynomial families for 4/n as historical identity catalogue
connection: L. Bernstein's 1962 paper on m/n = 1/x+1/y+1/z (esp. m = 4) gives families of solutions ↔ repo's identity tables.
why: Cross-check that the repo's identity catalogue includes Bernstein's families; may contain families on non-residue-class sets.
first_step: Check whether 'L. Bernstein, J. Reine Angew. Math. 211 (1962)' is the right citation and extract its families.

title: Sierpiński's 1956 monograph on decompositions into unit fractions
connection: Sierpiński 'Sur les décompositions de nombres rationnels en fractions primaires' ↔ early systematic treatment.
why: Classic sources sometimes contain lemmas or conjectures forgotten later.
first_step: Locate a scan (Mém. Soc. Math. France?) and skim for 4/n and 5/n material — check the citation first.

title: Mordell's 'Diophantine Equations' (1969) chapter on 4/n: his stated obstructions and hopes
connection: Mordell's book section where the mod-840 reduction appears ↔ his remarks on why identities can't cover squares.
why: Primary-source check of the Mordell–Schinzel narrative; might contain an overlooked suggestion.
first_step: Read the relevant section of Mordell's book and record his remarks verbatim (with page).

title: Dickson's History of the Theory of Numbers, vol. II, Egyptian-fraction chapter
connection: Dickson collects 19th-century work on unit-fraction equations ↔ pre-ES identities.
why: Cheap, may surface old parametrisations.
first_step: Skim Dickson vol. II chapter on 'sums of reciprocals' (archive.org) for equations 1/x+1/y+1/z = a/b.

title: Covering-radius analogy: CRT evasion as covering radius of a 'certificate code'
connection: Residue classes avoided by an adversarial p ↔ a word at maximal distance from a code; B1 = covering radius > 0 for any finite code.
why: Coding theory has tight covering-radius bounds; might quantify 'how many certificate classes needed to cover primes ≤ X' as a function of X.
first_step: Define code C_B = set of certificate class vectors for moduli ≤ B; compute empirically the fraction of residue vectors not covered as B grows (ties to set-cover item).

title: LLM-assisted literature mining for lemmas of shape 'a fixed integer has a divisor in a residue class'
connection: Semantic search across arXiv for any theorem guaranteeing a divisor of a specific integer in a specified class ↔ ES's core event.
why: Such lemmas are rare and scattered (e.g. in primitive divisor theory, cyclotomy); a targeted mining pass may find a forgotten one.
first_step: Run arXiv full-text search for phrases 'has a divisor congruent to', 'divisor in the residue class', 'prime factor congruent to -1' and screen hits.

title: Divisors ≡ −1 mod m of numbers ≡ 1 mod m: forced when the number has a 'twisted' structure (e.g. N = a² − b² with a ≡ 0, b ≡ 1?)
connection: If N = (A − 1)(A + 1)/k-type factorisations with A ≡ 0 mod m, then A − 1 ≡ −1 mod m is a divisor ↔ ES: 4Cp+1 = (A−1)(A+1)/… would need 4Cp + 1 + 1 = A²·… hmm: 4Cp+1 = d·d' with d ≡ d' ≡ −1 mod 4C; d = A − 1, d' = A' − 1.
why: Clarifies: ES Type II ⟺ 4Cp+1 = (4uC − 1)(4BC − 1); writing as difference of squares, 4Cp+1 = ((d+d')/2)² − ((d−d')/2)² — a representation as difference of squares with constraints mod 4C on the sum — a quadratic-form representation question.
first_step: Rewrite ES Type II as: 4Cp + 1 = X² − Y² with X ≡ −1 (mod 4C)... (X = (d+d')/2 ≡ −1 mod 2C) and test whether this binary-quadratic view yields anything beyond divisor form.

title: Fermat's factorisation viewpoint: 4Cp+1 + Y² must be a square X² with X ≡ −1 (mod 2C)
connection: Fermat's method searches X ≥ √N with X² − N square ↔ ES certificate as a Fermat factorisation step landing in a class.
why: Near-square factorisations (d ≈ d') correspond to small Y; the class condition on X is a congruence on a 'quadratic progression' X² − N, amenable to quadratic-sieve-style analysis.
first_step: For hard p, run Fermat-style search on 4Cp+1 for X ≡ −1 mod 2C up to X ≤ √N + K and count hits vs prediction.

title: Quadratic sieve / CFRAC structure: smooth values of X² − 4Cp − 1 as a thick object at p
connection: QS finds many smooth X² − N (thick object of size ~ N^{1/2} smooth values per sieve interval) ↔ combine smooth relations to get a factorisation of N with prescribed class of factors?
why: Combining relations yields congruences of squares, i.e. a nontrivial factor gcd(X − Y, N) — whose class mod 4C is uncontrolled. But one can sieve over C as well (many N): a 2D thick object.
first_step: Prototype: for C ≤ 50 run a tiny QS on 4Cp+1 and record the classes mod 4C of the factors found; is −1 hit at least as often as random?

title: Pocklington/Proth-style primality certificates as anti-certificates: when 4Cp+1 is prime, slice C fails
connection: Proth: N = k·2^n + 1 primality tests ↔ 4Cp+1 = (4C)·p + 1 is Pocklington-friendly (p | N − 1).
why: Every C with 4Cp+1 prime kills slice C; such C are certifiable cheaply. A counterexample prime p needs many such C or other failure modes; the density of 'Pocklington-prime C' for hard p is a measurable stress quantity.
first_step: Count C ≤ 10⁴ with 4Cp+1 prime for (★)-failing primes vs random primes; compare with Hardy–Littlewood prediction.

title: Cunningham-chain-like structures: p with 4p+1, 8p+1, 12p+1, … all prime or class-constrained
connection: Simultaneous primality of 4Cp+1 for C ≤ K (Dickson-type tuple) ↔ the B1 construction of hard primes.
why: Searching for primes with long runs of prime 4Cp+1 gives naturally hard test cases for (★) (not for ES itself).
first_step: Search p ≤ 10¹² for the longest run C = 1..K with every 4Cp+1 prime; compute R(p) and full ES count for the record holders.

title: Hypothesis-H-generated hard primes vs ES: do they also stress Type I?
connection: Dickson-tuple primes kill small (★) slices but Type I slices (divisors of p² + 4c²d) are different ↔ test whether Type I compensates.
why: If Type I is uncorrelated with the tuple construction, ES's union is robust to single-family adversaries — evidence on the 'independent families' model.
first_step: For the record primes from the previous item compute f_I(p) and compare with typical p.

title: Polynomial-time certificate algorithm conjecture: Type I trial divisions suffice within (log p)^3 steps
connection: Algorithmic version of ES ↔ a concrete deterministic algorithm with conjectured polylog running time.
why: A precise algorithmic conjecture is testable to large p via random sampling and invites complexity-theoretic analysis.
first_step: Define the algorithm (order trials by modulus), run on 10⁶ random primes near 10^30 (using trial division on candidate divisors only), record max steps / log³p.

title: ES 'with witnesses' certificate format and an independent checker
connection: Standardised certificate (p, x, y, z) plus type metadata ↔ verification hygiene for all experiments.
why: Prevents silent errors in large censuses; trivial but useful infrastructure.
first_step: Write scripts/es_check_cert.py verifying 4xyz = p(xy+yz+zx) with exact integers and classifying Type I/II.

title: Symmetric-function view: e₂/e₃ = 4/n and the power-sum moments of solutions
connection: For solutions (x,y,z), power sums p_k relate to e_i via Newton ↔ distribution of (x/p, y/p, z/p) shape statistics.
why: Shape statistics (e.g. ratios y/x) of all solutions across p might show a limiting distribution consistent with the main-term density; deviations hint at structure.
first_step: Compute the empirical distribution of (log y/log p, log z/log p) over all solutions for p ≤ 10⁵ and compare with the predicted density from parametrisations.

title: Egyptian-fraction 'tree of all solutions' as a graph: connected via common denominators
connection: Graph whose nodes are solutions for all n ≤ X, edges when they share two denominators ↔ moves between solutions of different n.
why: If moves are local (n changes by small structured amounts), the graph could support induction-like arguments (ES(n) from ES(n') via a move).
first_step: Build the graph for n ≤ 10⁴ and study components, degree distribution, and whether each prime connects to a smaller n by a short path.

title: Induction on p via 'certificate inheritance' along chains p → (p+1)/2 or similar
connection: Look for maps φ on primes with φ(p) < p such that ES(φ(p)) plus local data ⟹ ES(p) ↔ a descent/induction proof.
why: Most such maps fail (ES isn't hereditary) but checking simple candidate maps on data is cheap; a map that works empirically to 10⁸ would be surprising and informative.
first_step: Test candidate maps φ(p) ∈ {(p+3)/4, (p−1)/4 odd part, largest prime factor of p+3} for 'certificate transfer' rules on primes ≤ 10⁶.

title: Hereditary closure: ES(n) ⟹ ES(kn), so only primes matter — dualise: does ES(p) follow from ES of all p·q for many q?
connection: Reverse direction: solutions for pq (q varying prime) that are 'Type I in p' might descend ↔ thick family {pq : q prime} at fixed p.
why: This gives a thick object (all primes q) at fixed p; descent condition must be checked. A 'p-primitive' solution for pq with denominators all divisible by q descends.
first_step: For hard p, compute for q ≤ 1000 solutions of 4/(pq) where q divides all denominators (=> descends) vs other; check whether descending solutions exist exactly when ES(p) has certain types.

title: 4/p via 4/p = 1/p + 3/p and 3-term ES for 3/p with one term forced: ES ⟸ 3/p = 1/y + 1/z with p | …
connection: Taking x = p gives 3/p = 1/y + 1/z which by Rav needs divisors d₁+d₂ ≡ 0 mod 3 of p·k — fails for p ≡ 1 mod 3 often ↔ the 'x = p·t' slices (Type I) generalise.
why: Sanity item showing Type I slices are '(4t−1)/(pt) as a 2-term sum'; each t a binary problem with Rav criterion — exact per-t criterion via divisors of p·t·…
first_step: Write the Rav criterion for (4t−1)/(pt) and compute the per-t success probability vs t; compare with Type I counts.

title: Kernel-method / Gaussian process regression for R(p)/M(p) with arithmetic kernels
connection: Kernels k(p,q) based on shared residues (e.g. Σ_m w_m 1[p ≡ q mod m]) ↔ GP regression predicts R(p).
why: Learned kernel weights w_m identify the moduli that carry structure; residual variance quantifies randomness.
first_step: Fit a GP with arithmetic kernel on 10⁴ primes; inspect learned w_m.

title: Persistent homology of certificate point clouds
connection: TDA on the set of (log u, log C) certificates per p ↔ shape features (holes, clusters).
why: Speculative; might detect clustering patterns invisible in histograms.
first_step: Compute persistence diagrams for certificate clouds of 100 hard and 100 easy primes; compare with a permutation test.

title: Benchmark: build an 'ES-hard' dataset for AI provers (statements of sub-lemmas with known answers)
connection: AI-for-math benchmarks ↔ ES sub-lemmas (thin families, slice criteria, T1) with ground truth.
why: Gives the AI community a test bed tied to ES; attracts tool-builders.
first_step: Collect 30 sub-statements (PROVED ones with proofs, CERTIFIED computations, open ones) in a uniform format.

title: ES words are generalised Frobenius numbers: tuv − u − v = g_t(u,v), the largest integer with ≤ t−1 representations by ⟨u,v⟩ (CHECKED)
connection: For coprime u,v the largest n with at most t−1 representations n = au + bv (a,b ≥ 0) is tuv − u − v (t = 1: Sylvester's uv − u − v) ↔ I3/ES₅ words p = tuv − u − v, and (★) is t = 4C: p = 4C·uB − u − B.
why: Puts ES (★)/I3 inside the Frobenius problem / numerical-semigroup theory: ES(★) ⟺ p is the 4C-th 'k-Frobenius number' of some 2-generated semigroup ⟨u,B⟩. That field has its own tools (Apéry sets, Popoviciu's formula, Ehrhart theory, denumerants) and literature on which integers occur as (k-)Frobenius numbers. Not found in repo by grep.
first_step: Verified for u,v < 12, t ≤ 4 (scripts/z52b_free_opus_check3.py). Next: search literature for 'k-Frobenius number' / 'generalized Frobenius number two generators' (Beck–Robins; Brown et al., J. Integer Seq. 2010 — check) and for 'which integers are Frobenius numbers'.

title: Sylvester 1884 coin problem as the t = 1 ancestor of ES words: history link Sylvester ↔ Erdős–Straus
connection: Sylvester's Educational Times result (largest non-representable = uv − u − v) is the t = 1 case of the ES word shape tuv − u − v ↔ ES is a 'Sylvester-type' question about which primes are k-Frobenius numbers.
why: A historical bridge; the Frobenius-number literature (Ramírez Alfonsín's monograph) might have studied the inverse problem 'given n, find semigroups with g_k = n'.
first_step: Read Ramírez Alfonsín, 'The Diophantine Frobenius Problem' (OUP 2005) index for 'inverse problem' and 'k-Frobenius'; note any result on which integers are Frobenius numbers of 2-generated semigroups with multiplicity constraints.

title: Popoviciu's formula: N(n; a,b) = n/(ab) − {b′n/a} − {a′n/b} + 1 turns (★) into a sawtooth extremality condition
connection: Popoviciu: number of representations of n by ⟨a,b⟩ in terms of fractional parts with a′ ≡ a⁻¹ (mod b), b′ ≡ b⁻¹ (mod a) ↔ n is a k-Frobenius number iff both fractional parts take their maximum (a−1)/a, (b−1)/b, i.e. n ≡ −b (mod a) and n ≡ −a (mod b) (the pair form).
why: Links ES to sawtooth functions ((x)) and hence Dedekind sums and Dedekind/Rademacher reciprocity — reciprocity laws are exactly where T1-type parity information lives (repo's Dedekind–HJ charge was χ-blind; this is a different Dedekind-sum entry point via semigroup counting).
first_step: Write Σ over (u,B) of the Popoviciu sawtooth product for fixed p and check whether summing with weights yields a Dedekind-sum expression with a reciprocity-law evaluation.

title: Ehrhart / lattice points on dilated segments: N(p; u,B) as an Ehrhart quasi-polynomial value
connection: The denumerant N(n; u,B) counts lattice points on the segment {ux + By = n, x,y ≥ 0} — a rational polytope; its Ehrhart quasi-polynomial has period uB ↔ ES(★) ⟺ for some (u,B), the quasi-polynomial at n = p hits the 'minimal' constituent.
why: Ehrhart reciprocity relates N(n) and N(−n − u − B) (interior points); p = 4CuB − u − B means −p − u − B = −4CuB: the Ehrhart reciprocity partner of p is a multiple of uB — a crisp algebraic restatement of the (★) condition.
first_step: Verify via Ehrhart–Macdonald reciprocity: N(p) relates to the interior count at 4CuB; derive (★) ⟺ 'p's reciprocity partner is divisible by 4uB' and check numerically.

title: Apéry sets and the gap structure of ⟨u,B⟩: p as the maximal element of a 'level-(4C−1)' Apéry-type set
connection: Numerical semigroup S = ⟨u,B⟩: the set of n with exactly k representations has a known structure (shifted Apéry sets) ↔ p must be the top element of the k = 4C − 1 layer.
why: Semigroup-theoretic language may let one treat (u,B) as an unknown semigroup and p as a forced invariant — e.g. counting semigroups of given 'k-Frobenius number' (an inverse problem) could have a generating-function solution.
first_step: Compute, for n ≤ 10⁴, the number of pairs (u,B, t) with g_t(u,B) = n, t ≡ 0 mod 4, and compare with R(n); then look for a semigroup-enumeration generating function.

title: Counting numerical semigroups by Frobenius number (Backelin, Kaplan, Zhai) as a template for 'every p is a k-Frobenius number'
connection: The number of numerical semigroups with Frobenius number F grows like c·2^{F/2} (Backelin) ↔ here restricted to embedding dimension 2 (polylog many) with k-Frobenius.
why: The embedding-dimension-2 restriction collapses the count to divisor-type size (as expected); but allowing embedding dimension 3 semigroups (three generators) might correspond to richer ES-type certificates — check if a 3-generator k-Frobenius identity gives ES solutions.
first_step: Compute Frobenius numbers of 3-generated semigroups ⟨a,b,c⟩ in families and check whether some family's g(a,b,c) formula yields ES certificates (e.g. Type I parametrisation).

title: Type I as a Frobenius-type formula? Look for a semigroup interpretation of the Type I parametrisation
connection: Type II (★) is a 2-generator k-Frobenius identity ↔ Type I (f | p² + 4c²d …) may correspond to a different invariant (e.g. Frobenius number of ⟨a, b, c⟩ or genus of ⟨u,v⟩: genus = (u−1)(v−1)/2).
why: If Type I also has a semigroup meaning, ES would be 'p is one of a few semigroup invariants of some small semigroup' — a uniform language for all certificates.
first_step: Write the Type I solution family in ET variables and test whether p equals g_t, genus, or other standard invariants (e.g. number of gaps, conductor) of ⟨·,·⟩ with parameters from the solution.

title: Representation-count symmetry N(n) + N(g_t − n) = t on [0, g_t] (CHECKED): an involution attached to every ES word
connection: For coprime u,v and g_t = tuv − u − v, the denumerant satisfies N(n) + N(g_t − n) = t for all 0 ≤ n ≤ g_t (generalising symmetry of ⟨u,v⟩ at t = 1) ↔ every ES word p = g_t(u,v) carries the involution n ↦ p − n on representation data.
why: An explicit involution attached to each certificate is the raw material for windmill/parity arguments (G1 parity column); here the involution lives on representations of integers below p rather than on certificates — a different thick object (size ≍ p).
first_step: Verified for u,v ≤ 8, t ≤ 4 (scripts/z52b_free_opus_check3.py). Next: look for a global involution on pairs (n, representation) over all (u,v) whose fixed points correspond to certificates of p; test fixed-point parity on p < 10³.

title: Which integers are k-Frobenius numbers of ⟨u,v⟩ with k ≡ 3 (mod 4): a direct elementary question to post
connection: Restating (★) without Egyptian fractions: 'every prime p ≡ 1 (4) except 14 known ≤ 10¹⁰ is the largest integer having exactly 4C−1 representations by some coprime pair u,v'.
why: Semigroup/Frobenius community (e.g. García-Sánchez, Rosales, Ramírez Alfonsín) may recognise it; experts in that field are not in the ES network.
first_step: Draft a short note/MO post in Frobenius language with data, clearly marking that (★) is sufficient for ES but not equivalent (user approval before posting).

title: Frobenius-problem algorithms (Kannan, Barvinok short generating functions) for counting certificates
connection: Barvinok's algorithm counts lattice points in rational polytopes in polynomial time in fixed dimension via short rational generating functions ↔ R(p) as lattice-point count in a union of polytopes indexed by (u,B).
why: Short generating functions might give an exact closed form for Σ_{u,B ≤ U} N-type counts; ES's union over unbounded (u,B) is the issue but truncations are exact objects.
first_step: Use LattE to compute the generating function of {(u,B,C) : 4uBC − u − B = n} truncated at u,B ≤ U and compare with direct counts.

title: Erdős–Kac over C at fixed p: distribution of ω(4Cp+1) for C ≤ X is a genuine fixed-p average
connection: For fixed p, 4Cp+1 (C ≤ X) is an AP with modulus 4p; small prime factors q ≤ X distribute like random ↔ a Turán–Kubilius/Erdős–Kac theorem over C at fixed p is provable for prime factors up to X.
why: Fixed-p averages over C are legitimate thick objects (no averaging over p); what fails is controlling the class of factors mod 4C. Making this precise documents exactly which fixed-p statements are provable.
first_step: Prove (or find in literature) Turán–Kubilius for {4Cp+1 : C ≤ X} counting prime factors q ≤ X^{1/2}; then state the strongest 'class' statement this gives (likely only for prime factors q with q ≡ −1 mod 4C, q ≤ X: the small-prime-certificate family).

title: Chebyshev-bias analogue: are certain classes mod 840·k systematically harder?
connection: Prime number races / Chebyshev bias ↔ per-class average of R(p)/M(p) among the six Mordell-hard classes mod 840 and their lifts.
why: Systematic class biases indicate local factors not yet in M_BM — refinement of the main term or new local invariant.
first_step: Compute mean R(p)/M_BM(p) per class mod 840·11·13 for primes ≤ 10⁸ and test for significant deviations.

title: Grechuk's systematic catalogue of Diophantine equations: where does 4xyz = n(xy+yz+zx) sit?
connection: B. Grechuk's book/papers order polynomial Diophantine equations by size and record solved/open status ↔ ES family and its nearest solved neighbours by 'size'.
why: Nearby equations in a size-ordered catalogue that were solved suggest methods; ES-like families with parameter n might appear among his open problems.
first_step: Check whether Grechuk, 'Polynomial Diophantine Equations: A Systematic Approach' (Springer, 2024) exists as cited, and look up equations of the form axyz = n(xy+yz+zx) or xyz − x − y = n there.

title: Sibling: n = xyz − x − y − z (and n = xyz − x − y) universality thresholds
connection: I3: n = tuv − u − v with t,u,v ≥ 3 covers all n > 2 433 600 ↔ sibling shapes xyz − x − y − z, xyz + x + y may have their own exception lists and known proofs.
why: Sibling exception structures calibrate I3_𝒞 (repo's ES-strength conjecture); a sibling with a provable finite exception list would be a method precedent.
first_step: Compute exceptions of n = xyz − x − y − z with x,y,z ≥ 2 up to 10⁷; inspect whether the exception set is finite-looking and whether it has a T1-like obstruction (squares?).

title: Mining the repo's ~470 brainstorm memos for dangling 'first steps' never executed
connection: Many memos end with proposed cheap tests ↔ some were never run.
why: Executing forgotten cheap tests is high-yield housekeeping.
first_step: Grep BRAINSTORM/*.md for 'first step', 'cheap test', 'TODO', 'next:' and cross-check against data/ and scripts/ for evidence of execution; list unexecuted ones.

title: Project Euler Egyptian-fraction problems as a source of fast counting algorithms
connection: PE problems on 1/x + 1/y = 1/n and related count solutions fast via divisor enumeration ↔ certificate enumeration engineering.
why: Algorithmic tricks (e.g. enumerating divisors of n² quickly) may speed up censuses.
first_step: Review PE problem forums for unit-fraction problems' best algorithms; benchmark against repo's census code.

title: Decision-tree lower bound: any certificate search querying 'm | p + u' needs ≥ … queries in the worst case
connection: Adversary arguments in query complexity ↔ B1 CRT evasion as an adversary strategy.
why: Formalises B1 as a query-complexity statement: any algorithm with a fixed query order needs unbounded queries (under Dickson); clarifies that the obstacle is order-independent.
first_step: Write the adversary argument formally under Hypothesis H and state the lower bound in terms of menu size.

title: ES over the Eisenstein integers (first sextant) as a new failure-calibrated sibling
connection: ES_Q1 over ℤ[i] has 6 genuine prime failures ↔ an Eisenstein analogue (denominators in a 60° sector) gives another sibling for the zero-law fit.
why: More siblings with observed failures improve the calibration of P(ES false) (G4).
first_step: Adapt scripts/z52_bank_gauss.c to ℤ[ω] with denominators in the closed sector arg ∈ [0, π/3]; list failures for N(n) ≤ 10⁴.

title: Kummer-theory view of the class gate: −1 as product of factor classes ⟺ splitting in a ray class field
connection: d ≡ −1 (mod 4C) for d | N ⟺ the Artin symbol of the ideal (d) in ℚ(ζ_{4C}) equals complex conjugation ↔ ES Type II asks: does 4Cp+1 have a divisor whose Frobenius in Gal(ℚ(ζ_{4C})/ℚ) is complex conjugation?
why: Rephrases the class gate in Galois terms: 'some divisor of N_C has Frobenius = complex conjugation in the 4C-th cyclotomic field' — a Chebotarev-type event for divisors of a single integer; complex conjugation being the target ties nicely to positivity (the real place).
first_step: Write the condition for the d-part using ideals of ℚ(ζ_{4C})⁺ (real subfield): d ≡ −1 means d's Frobenius is trivial in the real subfield and nontrivial in ℚ(ζ_{4C}) — split completely in ℚ(ζ_{4C})⁺ but not in ℚ(ζ_{4C}). Test whether this suggests using the real cyclotomic field's units.

title: Real cyclotomic subfield ℚ(ζ_{4C})⁺: divisors split there but inert/ramified-ish in the CM extension
connection: From previous: d ≡ −1 (mod 4C) ⟺ d ≡ ±1 (split in ℚ(ζ_{4C})⁺ for primes) and not +1 ↔ the CM extension ℚ(ζ_{4C})/ℚ(ζ_{4C})⁺ and its relative class group / Stickelberger.
why: CM-field arithmetic (relative class numbers, Stickelberger) is a rigid R-type toolbox; ES's '−1 not +1' distinction is a CM-type sign, possibly linked to the BM character χ_{−4uB}.
first_step: For small C, express R(p)'s C-slice via characters of Gal(ℚ(ζ_{4C})/ℚ) odd under complex conjugation; check whether the odd characters' contribution is a relative-class-number-like quantity.

title: Odd vs even characters split of the slice count: R_C(p) = even part + odd part
connection: 1[d ≡ −1] = (1/φ) Σ_χ χ(−1)χ̄(d)… = (even-χ sum − odd-χ sum)/φ(4C) applied to Σ_{d|N} ↔ even part = count of d ≡ ±1, odd part = signed difference #(≡ −1) − #(≡ +1) among d ≡ ±1.
why: Since N ≡ 1 mod 4C and d ↦ N/d preserves ±1 classes, the odd part is a signed divisor count (like r₂); if a closed form exists, it's an exact charge identity per slice.
first_step: Compute for each C ≤ 30 and p ≤ 10⁵ the signed count #{d|N: d≡−1} − #{d|N: d≡+1} and look for multiplicative closed forms.

title: Triangle orbifolds: ES(n) ⟺ a hyperbolic triangle group Δ(x,y,z) has area 2π(1 − 4/n)
connection: Orbifold Euler characteristic of S²(x,y,z) is 1/x + 1/y + 1/z − 1, so ES(n) ⟺ some triangle orbifold has χ = 4/n − 1 (hyperbolic for n > 4), i.e. area 2π(n−4)/n ↔ the area spectrum of hyperbolic triangle groups.
why: Exact dictionary (folklore-level, not in repo by grep): ES asks which rationals 1 − 4/n lie in the area spectrum {1 − 1/x − 1/y − 1/z} of triangle groups. Triangle groups bring Riemann–Hurwitz, dessins d'enfants (finite-index subgroups), and Fuchsian-group combinatorics; by Riemann–Hurwitz a genus-g surface with a G-action of signature (x,y,z) has 2g − 2 = |G|(n − 4)/n, so p | |G| for prime n = p.
first_step: Search literature for 'set of areas / Euler characteristics of triangle orbifolds' and 'which rationals are orbifold Euler characteristics of genus-0 three-point orbifolds'; record any density/representability theorem.

title: Rigidity reading: 3 cone points (triangle groups) are rigid, 4 cone points have moduli — mirrors 3-term ES hard vs 4-term easy
connection: Teichmüller space of S²(x₁,…,x_k) has dimension 2k − 6: zero for triangle groups, positive for 4 or more cone points ↔ ES with 3 terms is hard while the 4-term analogue is easy.
why: A heuristic link between geometric rigidity and arithmetic sparsity (polylog solutions). It suggests looking for 'deformation' arguments that start from a 4-cone-point solution (always available) and degenerate a cone point (order → ∞ or merging) to reach 3 points.
first_step: Write the degeneration: 4/p = 1/a + 1/b + 1/c + 1/d with d → merging (1/c + 1/d = 1/e) — count how often a 4-term solution has two terms merging to a unit fraction (same as batch A's 4→3 collapse item; check the geometric version gives anything new).

title: Dessins d'enfants of type (x,y,z) with χ = 4/p − 1: ES certificates as Belyi maps
connection: Finite-index subgroups of Δ(x,y,z) ↔ dessins (bipartite maps) with all white-vertex degrees dividing x, etc. ↔ an ES certificate is the 'type' of a dessin whose Euler-characteristic bookkeeping involves p.
why: Dessins carry a Galois action; if an ES certificate could be read off a canonical dessin attached to p (e.g. from a Belyi map of a curve with p-torsion), existence would be algebraic. Speculative.
first_step: Look for a natural Belyi map attached to p (e.g. on the Fermat curve of exponent p, or X(p)) whose passport (ramification type) gives (x,y,z) with 1/x + 1/y + 1/z = 4/p; X₀(p)-type modular curves have ramification (2,3,∞) — check others.

title: Weighted projective line: ES(★) ⟺ O(p) ≅ ω ⊗ π*O_{P¹}(4C) on the stacky curve P(u,B)
connection: On P(u,B) one has h⁰(O(n)) = N(n; u,B) (denumerant), ω = O(−u−B), and O(uB) = π*O(1) from the coarse P¹ ↔ p = 4C·uB − u − B is exactly deg(ω) + 4C·deg(π*O(1)).
why: Puts (★) into algebraic-geometry language where Riemann–Roch/Serre duality on stacky curves is the Popoviciu formula and the denumerant symmetry N(n)+N(g_t−n) = t is Serre duality. Type I might then correspond to stacky curves with three orbifold points — a uniform geometric home for both types.
first_step: Verify the Serre-duality derivation of N(n) + N(g_t − n) = t on P(u,B); then test whether Type I certificates correspond to line bundles of the form ω ⊗ (pullback) on P(a,b,c)-type stacky curves (three orbifold points).

title: 2D quantum harmonic oscillator: (★) ⟺ in an oscillator with frequencies (u,B), level p is the highest level with degeneracy 4C − 1
connection: Energy levels n = au + bB of a 2D oscillator with commensurate frequencies have degeneracy N(n; u,B) ↔ ES words p = g_t(u,B) are 'last levels before the degeneracy reaches t' (with particle–hole-type symmetry N(n) + N(g_t − n) = t).
why: Exact physics dictionary; degeneracy-counting via semiclassical (Weyl) asymptotics plus exact Ehrhart corrections is a mature toolkit. Mostly a reframing, but the 'degeneracy jump' language may suggest spectral (trace-formula) approaches to counting all (u,B) at once.
first_step: Write Z(β) = Σ_n N(n;u,B) e^{−βn} = 1/((1 − e^{−βu})(1 − e^{−βB})) and express 'p is a jump level' via residues of Z at roots of unity (Sylvester waves); sum over (u,B) formally.

title: Sylvester waves of the restricted partition function p_{u,B}(n) evaluated at n = p
connection: Sylvester decomposed restricted partition functions into waves (polynomial part + periodic parts from roots of unity of order dividing u, B) ↔ the (★) condition is that the periodic waves of order u and B both take their extreme values at p.
why: Wave decomposition writes the condition as a sum of root-of-unity terms — a Fourier expansion over e^{2πi k/u}, e^{2πi l/B} — possibly summable over (u,B) to an exponential-sum expression for R(p).
first_step: Write the Sylvester wave for two parts explicitly (via Rademacher/Dedekind–Fourier sums) and derive R(p) as a double sum over (u,B) of root-of-unity sums; check numerically for small p.

title: Seifert fibred spaces: ES(n) ⟺ a Seifert space over S²(x,y,z) with all β_i = 1 has rational Euler number −4/n
connection: For M = M(0; (x,1),(y,1),(z,1)) the rational Euler number is e = −(1/x + 1/y + 1/z) and |H₁(M)| = |e|·xyz = xy + yz + zx ↔ ES(n) ⟺ such an M has e = −4/n; equivalently the Montesinos link M(1/x,1/y,1/z) has double branched cover with these invariants.
why: Imports 3-manifold topology (Seifert invariants, Montesinos links, Casson–Walker invariants given by Dedekind sums) — another home for reciprocity-type obstructions like T1; |H₁| = xy + yz + zx ties to the ES numerator identity 4xyz = n(xy+yz+zx).
first_step: Check the sign conventions and the |H₁| formula for Seifert rational homology spheres; then compute linking forms of these M for ES solutions at odd squares vs primes and see whether T1 appears as a linking-form condition.

title: Lens spaces and linear plumbings: ES₅'s continued-fraction length ≤ 3 as 'L(p,q) bounds a 3-vertex linear plumbing'
connection: The negative continued fraction of p/q gives the linear plumbing whose boundary is L(p,q) ↔ ES₅: a p-tied rational with CF length ≤ 3 (with congruence constraints) ⟹ some L(p,q) is the boundary of a ≤ 3-vertex plumbing with constrained weights.
why: Lens space surgery theory (which lens spaces come from surgery on knots; Moser's torus-knot surgeries) is a rich classification; a match between ES₅'s constraints and a topological condition would bring Heegaard Floer / lattice-embedding obstructions (Lisca-style) into play.
first_step: Translate the repo's ES₅ CF-length-3 condition precisely into plumbing weights (−a₁, −a₂, −a₃) and check whether the congruence constraints correspond to a natural topological property (e.g. spin structure, lattice embedding).

title: Torus knots T(u,B): 2g(T(u,B)) = (u−1)(B−1) and the (★) relation p + 1 = 2g + (4C−1)uB
connection: The semigroup ⟨u,B⟩ is the semigroup of the plane-curve singularity x^u = y^B (link = torus knot); its conductor is 2g = (u−1)(B−1) ↔ (★): p = 4CuB − u − B ⟺ p + 1 − 2g(T(u,B)) = (4C − 1)uB.
why: Links (★) to singularity theory (Milnor number μ = 2g) and knot invariants (Alexander polynomial exponents = semigroup); speculative, but singularity theory has deformation/adjacency structures that might act on certificates.
first_step: Check the identity and ask whether the condition '(p + 1 − μ) ≡ 0 mod uB with quotient ≡ 3 mod 4' has a meaning for the Milnor fibre or for the Alexander polynomial evaluated at roots of unity.

title: Coxeter triangle groups: hyperbolic triangle with angles π/x, π/y, π/z has area π(1 − 4/n)
connection: Same dictionary as triangle orbifolds, in reflection-group form ↔ ES(n) ⟺ a hyperbolic Coxeter triangle of area π(n − 4)/n with angles π/x, π/y, π/z.
why: Coxeter-group language may be more familiar to some communities (geometric group theory); also hyperbolic tessellations {x,y,z} pictures for outreach.
first_step: Render the Coxeter triangle tessellations for a few ES solutions of 4/p (outreach) and check whether the 'arithmetic' triangle groups (Takeuchi's finite list) ever give ES certificates.

title: Takeuchi's arithmetic triangle groups: which ES certificates (x,y,z) are arithmetic?
connection: Takeuchi classified the 85 arithmetic hyperbolic triangle groups ↔ ES solutions (x,y,z) for small n that are arithmetic triangle types.
why: Curiosity: arithmetic certificates would carry quaternion-algebra structure (cf. repo's quaternion forms); likely only finitely many n, so it's a calibration not a route.
first_step: Intersect Takeuchi's list with {(x,y,z) : 1/x + 1/y + 1/z = 4/n} and list the n obtained.

title: Polyhedral/tiling vertex equations as Egyptian equations: classification precedents
connection: Vertex-configuration equations of tilings (e.g. Σ 1/k_i = const for polygons meeting at a vertex) are Egyptian-fraction equations solved by finite enumeration ↔ ES is the same algebra with an n-dependent right side.
why: Shows ES as 'a tiling-vertex equation at curvature 4/n'; mostly orientation, but hyperbolic tiling enumeration software could enumerate ES-type configurations quickly.
first_step: Write the angle condition for three regular polygons at a vertex of a hyperbolic tiling with prescribed angle defect and relate to 1/x + 1/y + 1/z = 4/n.

title: CM elliptic curve reading of prime certificates: q ≡ −1 (mod 4C) ⟺ 4C | #E(F_q) for y² = x³ − x at supersingular q
connection: For E: y² = x³ − x and primes q ≡ 3 (mod 4), #E(F_q) = q + 1, so a prime divisor q of 4Cp+1 is a certificate (q ≡ −1 mod 4C) iff 4C | #E(F_q) ↔ the class gate becomes a statement about group orders of a fixed CM curve modulo divisors of 4Cp+1.
why: Elliptic-curve group orders bring ECM-style 'scalar multiplication mod N' tests and division-field Chebotarev structure; a global point/isogeny argument forcing some prime factor of 4Cp+1 to have 4C | #E(F_q) would be a certificate. Speculative but exact for prime certificates.
first_step: Check the claim for q ≡ 3 mod 4 (supersingular ⟹ #E(F_q) = q+1) and extend to composite certificates d (product of primes in ±1 classes); then test whether computing [4C]·P on E mod N = 4Cp+1 detects certificate primes faster than factoring.

title: Parity-problem diagnosis: how strongly does slice success correlate with λ(4Cp+1)?
connection: Selberg's parity barrier: sieves cannot detect the parity of Ω ↔ slice C fails whenever 4Cp+1 is prime (λ = −1); if success is strongly parity-correlated, ES inherits the parity problem.
why: If ES-type events are parity-sensitive, sieve-only proofs are excluded for a structural reason (complementing B1/B2); if not, the obstruction lies elsewhere.
first_step: For p ≤ 10⁶ and C ≤ 50, compute P(slice succeeds | λ(4Cp+1) = ±1) and P(… | Ω = k).

title: Large-q limit of ES over F_q[T]: equidistribution (Katz/Deligne) at fixed degree may give a pointwise-in-polynomial theorem
connection: Function-field problems in the limit q → ∞ with fixed degree reduce to Chebotarev/monodromy computations (Katz–Sarnak style) ↔ ES over F_q[T] for every prime polynomial P of degree d once q ≫_d 1.
why: This is the kind of 'every element' theorem the integers lack; whether the monodromy group is large enough (and how T1 appears for square P) would show precisely what structure is responsible — a clean model of the missing integer input.
first_step: Check the repo's F_q[T] treatment: is it fixed q or q → ∞? If not done, compute the monodromy of the divisor-class event for Type II slices over F_q(T) for small d.

title: ES certificates for record-size Mordell-hard primes (Proth/generalised Fermat primes in square classes mod 840)
connection: Find a known huge prime p (≥ 10⁵ digits) in a Mordell-hard class and search small certificates (4uC−1) | p + u by trial division ↔ ES verified at a 'random' gigantic prime.
why: Cheap, publicity-friendly, and an adversarial data point at astronomically large p (does a small certificate always exist? the model predicts ≍ log² p ≈ 10¹¹ certificates but small ones are what is cheap to find).
first_step: Take primes from the Top-20 Proth list, reduce mod 840 to find one in a hard class, and run trial division of p + u by 4uC − 1 for uC ≤ 10⁶ using GMP.

title: Euler-type prime-generating polynomials as thin families (n² + n + 41 and relatives)
connection: Values of n² + n + 41 are prime for n ≤ 39; families with high prime density concentrate primes with special splitting (class number 1 field ℚ(√−163)) ↔ a thin family with rigid arithmetic.
why: Rigid splitting (every small prime is inert in ℚ(√−163)) is exactly the 'all small q are QNR-like' structure that affects F_q forcing lines; checking R on this family probes that interaction.
first_step: Compute R(p)/M_BM(p) for primes p = n² + n + 41 ≡ 1 mod 4 (n ≤ 10⁵) vs random primes.

title: Self-similarity: does R(p) for p in the hardest classes look like R of smaller primes rescaled (renormalisation in modulus)?
connection: Compare the distribution of R(p)/M(p) within p ≡ 1 mod 840 with that within p ≡ 1 mod 840·k for growing k ↔ scale-invariance of difficulty.
why: If deeper residue restriction keeps reducing R/M without bound, extremely structured primes could be dangerous (quantifies B1 drift); if it saturates, ES is robust.
first_step: Compute mean R/M over primes ≤ 10⁸ in nested classes p ≡ 1 mod 840, 840·11, 840·11·13, … (all-QR classes) and plot vs modulus.

title: Universal vs per-prime certificate menus: minimal menu covering all primes in [X, 2X]
connection: Set cover over a dyadic block ↔ how menu size must grow with X (B1 says unbounded).
why: The growth law of the minimal menu (e.g. ~ log X or ~ (log X)²) is a quantitative replacement for the qualitative B1 and could be compared with the CRT-adversary cost.
first_step: Greedy set cover for primes ≡ 1 mod 24 in [10^k, 2·10^k], k = 4..8, with menu items = (u,C) pairs; fit menu size vs k.

title: Interval version: every interval [X, X + (log X)^A] contains a prime with a certificate of size ≤ (log X)^B (provable?)
connection: Weak 'short-interval almost-everywhere' statement ↔ provable by first-moment counting if primes in short intervals were available — they're not at polylog length; restate with integers instead of primes.
why: Calibrates exactly which weak pointwise-in-intervals statements are provable; an integer (not prime) version may be elementary.
first_step: Prove: every interval [X, X + H] with H = (log X)^A contains an integer n ≡ 1 mod 4 with ES(n) via a small certificate (e.g. via n ≡ −u mod 4uC−1 for small fixed (u,C) — CRT gives density, so trivially yes for H ≥ 4uC−1). Record that it's trivial for integers and impossible-to-state for primes at this length.

title: Pólya–Vinogradov-scale improvement for T(p) using the Frobenius/Popoviciu structure
connection: M_BM lower bound uses Burgess/PV on T(p) = Σ (−uB/p)/φ(4uB) ↔ in Frobenius language the weights 1/φ(4uB) and pair (u,B) have semigroup structure that might allow summation by parts in a better order.
why: Better constants in M_BM ≥ c log² p are concrete, publishable-grade improvements (even though ES itself needs R, not M).
first_step: Re-derive Theorem 2.2's constant and test numerically how close T(p)/M₀(p) gets to its worst case; identify which (u,B) ranges dominate the error.

title: Generating 'ES-like' random problems with tunable expected count to locate the existence threshold empirically
connection: Synthetic problems: replace p by random integers in classes and restrict menu so expected count μ varies ↔ empirical P(no solution) as a function of μ.
why: Gives an empirical law P(0) ≈ f(μ) for ES-shaped problems; plugging μ ≈ M_BM(p) estimates the risk at any p and calibrates the (J)97 zero law independently of siblings.
first_step: For random odd n ≡ 1 mod 24 up to 10⁸, count (★) certificates with u,B ≤ U for varying U (thus varying μ) and fit P(R_U = 0) vs μ.

title: Ask the LLM-board for 'connections we would be embarrassed to have missed' after merging z52b lanes
connection: Cross-model review of the merged list ↔ blind-spot detection.
why: Different models have different associative priors; a short adversarial 'what is missing' round is cheap.
first_step: After merge, run one board round with the prompt 'list 30 connections to ES absent from this list' and dedupe.
